problem.title: Hardcoded credentials are a ticking time bomb
problem.subtitle: Each risk below maps to well-established industry frameworks: NIST SP 800-53 / 800-207, MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP and CIS Controls.

items.title: Credentials in source code
items.desc: Hardcoded database passwords and API keys leak through git history, forks and CI logs: the most common unsecured-credential technique in MITRE ATT&CK (T1552.001) and a top weakness in CWE-798. Verizon's DBIR consistently ranks stolen credentials as the #1 breach vector.

items.title: No rotation
items.desc: Static credentials that never expire violate NIST SP 800-53 IA-5 (Authenticator Management) and NIST SP 800-63B guidance. A single leak grants standing access (MITRE ATT&CK T1078, Valid Accounts) until someone manually intervenes.

items.title: No audit trail
items.desc: Who read which secret, and when? Without centralized access logging you cannot satisfy NIST SP 800-53 AU-2 / AU-12, CIS Control 8 or PCI DSS Req. 10, and you cannot detect credential misuse.

problem.solution_title: Dynamic secrets with Palo Alto Networks | IDIRA Secrets Manager
problem.solution_desc: Secrets Manager flips the model: a workload never holds a static password. Each one authenticates with its own platform identity (a Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWT, a GitHub OIDC token or an AWS IAM role) and receives a short-lived secret, scoped by policy, fetched at runtime over mTLS and rotated automatically with zero downtime. No secret is ever written to source, a container image or an environment variable. The result is identity-first, least-privilege, fully-audited access (exactly the model prescribed by NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture) and it directly mitigates the MITRE ATT&CK techniques above (T1552.001 Credentials in Files, T1078 Valid Accounts).

pillars.title: Ephemeral identity, not passwords
pillars.desc: Every workload proves who it is with a JWT, OIDC token or IAM role: there is no shared, long-lived credential to steal.

pillars.title: Least privilege by policy
pillars.desc: Each identity reads only the secrets its Conjur policy explicitly grants, nothing more, enforced centrally.

pillars.title: Automatic rotation
pillars.desc: Short-TTL secrets are fetched at runtime and rotated with no downtime, so any leak expires on its own.

pillars.title: Complete audit trail
pillars.desc: Every secret retrieval is logged (who, what and when) ready for your SIEM and compliance evidence.

flow.diagram_label: SDK use case: the application authenticates to IDIRA Secrets Manager and fetches its own secrets
flow.s1_title: 1. The application needs a database password
flow.s1_desc: In the SDK pattern the application itself talks to IDIRA Secrets Manager. There is no password in the code, in the image or in a config file: the app will prove who it is and ask for the secret at run time.
flow.s2_title: 2. Kubernetes gives the pod an identity
flow.s2_desc: Kubernetes projects a short-lived ServiceAccount JWT into the pod. The application reads it from /var/run/secrets/tokens/jwt. This token is the app's identity, not a secret it has to protect.
flow.s3_desc: The app POSTs the JWT to the authn-jwt authenticator (service eks-latam). Secrets Manager checks the signature, issuer and audience, and maps the token to a workload identity defined in policy.
flow.s4_title: 4. Secrets Manager returns an access token
flow.s4_desc: If the JWT is valid, the app receives a short-lived API access token. Every following request carries it in the Authorization header.
flow.s5_desc: With the token, the app GETs three variables: username, password and address under data/vault/. Policy allows only what this identity was granted; the values stay in memory with a 5-minute TTL.
flow.s6_desc: The app builds the JDBC URL from the cached values and opens the connection. The UI only ever shows masked values.
flow.s7_title: 7. The cache serves the next requests
flow.s7_desc: For the next 5 minutes every request reads the in-memory cache, protected by double-checked locking, so Secrets Manager receives one call per TTL instead of one per request.
flow.s8_desc: When the cache expires, the app reads the current JWT (Kubernetes rotates it automatically), authenticates again and fetches fresh values. A password rotated in the vault reaches the app on the next cycle, with no redeploy.

flow.diagram_label: How GitHub Actions gets secrets with OIDC
flow.s1_title: A pipeline with no stored credentials
flow.s1_desc: The GitHub Actions job proves who it is with a token GitHub issues on the fly. IDIRA Secrets Manager trusts that token only for one repository and workflow, and hands back just the secrets that job may use.
flow.s2_desc: The workflow declares permissions id-token: write, which lets the job ask GitHub for an identity token. It runs on a self-hosted runner with the Secrets Manager action aslancarlos/workshop-action.
flow.s3_desc: The action requests a token from GitHub's OIDC provider. The JWT is signed by GitHub, lives a few minutes and carries claims such as repository and workflow.
flow.s4_desc: The action posts the JWT to authn-jwt/github. There is no API key, password or PAT in the repository or in GitHub Secrets.
flow.s5_desc: Secrets Manager fetches GitHub's public keys (JWKS) and checks the signature, issuer, audience and expiry. A forged or expired token stops here.
flow.s6_desc: The host identity has annotations for repository and workflow. Only aslancarlos/workshop-action running workshop-action matches; any other repository or workflow is denied. On a match the action gets a short-lived access token.
flow.s7_title: Only the scoped secrets come back
flow.s7_desc: With the access token the action fetches DB_USER, DB_PASS and DB_HOST. They become environment variables masked in every log line.
flow.s8_title: The job uses them and they vanish
flow.s8_desc: The job connects to MySQL with the fetched credentials. When the run ends the values are gone: nothing was stored on the runner, in the repository or in the pipeline.

flow.diagram_label: How the External Secrets Operator delivers secrets
flow.s1_title: Four players, zero vault code in the app
flow.s1_desc: The External Secrets Operator (ESO) runs in the cluster and copies secrets from IDIRA Secrets Manager into a normal Kubernetes Secret. The app only reads environment variables, and a small Python operator restarts it when a credential changes.
flow.s2_desc: An ExternalSecret resource lists the secrets to copy (DB_USER, DB_PASS and DB_HOST from data/vault/dev-demo-aslan/dbuser_dual) and how often: every minute. The ESO controller picks it up through the ClusterSecretStore conjur-store.
flow.s3_desc: The store authenticates with the springboot-app ServiceAccount. Kubernetes issues a short-lived JWT for it with the audience conjur, so no API key is stored anywhere.
flow.s4_desc: ESO posts the JWT to authn-jwt/eks-latam. Secrets Manager checks the signature, issuer and audience against the cluster, then returns a short-lived access token.
flow.s5_desc: With the token, ESO asks for the three variables. Policy confirms this identity may read them, and the vault returns the current values.
flow.s6_desc: ESO writes the values into the Secret eso-shop-db-creds and keeps it in sync. From here on it is standard Kubernetes: nothing in the cluster needs to know about the vault.
flow.s7_title: The app just reads env vars
flow.s7_desc: The ESO Shop pods load the Secret with envFrom and connect to MySQL. The Node.js code has no SDK, no sidecar and no secret in the image.
flow.s8_desc: When the password rotates in the vault, the next refresh (within a minute) brings the new value and ESO updates the Secret. No pipeline, no manual step.
flow.s9_desc: Environment variables are read only at start, so the Python operator watches the Secret through the Kubernetes Watch API. On a change it triggers a rolling restart with maxUnavailable 0, and the PodDisruptionBudget keeps 2 of 3 pods serving.

dual.title: Zero-Downtime Credential Rotation
dual.subtitle: Two accounts, one always active, and two ways to consume them. Follow IDIRA Dual Accounts serving the same credential to an application through the Credential Provider and to Kubernetes pods through Secrets Manager and the External Secrets Operator, with zero downtime during rotation.
dual.keyboard_hint: ← → steps · Space play/pause · drag the timeline to scrub
dual.key1_desc: CPM only changes the password of the inactive account, and only after the grace period. The account your consumers are using stays valid the whole time: no blackout window during rotation.
dual.key2_title: Size the GracePeriod for the Slowest Path
dual.key2_desc: GracePeriod (minutes, set on the rotational group platform) must cover every consumer's refresh. CyberArk recommends at least 3× the Credential Provider CacheRefreshInterval; for Kubernetes, add the Synchronizer sync (1 min), the ESO refreshInterval and the rollout time.
dual.key3_title: Ask for the Pair, Not the Account
dual.key3_desc: Consumers reference the VirtualUserName: a CP query (VirtualUserName=dbuser_dual) or the Secrets Manager variable data/vault/<safe>/dbuser_dual/password. Both always resolve to the Active account.
dual.s1_title: The Setup: One Name, Two Accounts
dual.s1_desc: Account A (Index 1) and Account B (Index 2) have identical permissions and are both enabled on the MySQL database. In the Vault they share the same VirtualUserName, dbuser_dual, and belong to one rotational group: the DualAccountStatus property tags A as Active and B as Inactive. Two very different consumers use this same pair.
dual.s2_desc: The application never asks for a specific account: it queries the Credential Provider for VirtualUserName=dbuser_dual. The CP answers from its local cache with whichever account is Active (Account A) and the app logs in to MySQL as appuser_01. The cache is refreshed from the Vault every CacheRefreshInterval.
dual.s3_title: Path 2: Kubernetes via Secrets Manager and ESO
dual.s3_desc: Every minute the Vault Synchronizer copies the pair into Secrets Manager as data/vault/<safe>/dbuser_dual/username and /password: always the Active account's values. The External Secrets Operator reads them every refreshInterval (1m) and writes the Kubernetes Secret eso-shop-db-creds; the ESO Shop pods load it through envFrom and also log in as appuser_01.
dual.s4_title: CPM Detects the Rotation Is Due
dual.s4_desc: Based on the rotational group platform settings, the Central Policy Manager (CPM) determines that the pair needs a password change. Dual Accounts rotation is performed by the CPM only: the Secrets Rotation service does not support it. No password has been touched yet.
dual.s5_title: The Status Swap: A → Inactive, B → Active
dual.s5_desc: CPM switches DualAccountStatus on both accounts, updates the group's CurrInd to Account B's index and marks the now-inactive Account A for a password change, delayed by the GracePeriod. Nothing breaks: the CP cache and the Secrets Manager variables still hand out Account A, whose password is still valid.
dual.s6_title: Grace Period: the Credential Provider Switches to B
dual.s6_desc: On its next cache refresh the Credential Provider picks up the new Active account. The same query for dbuser_dual now returns Account B, and the application logs in as appuser_02: no code change, no restart.
dual.s7_title: Grace Period: Kubernetes Switches to B
dual.s7_desc: Within a minute the Vault Synchronizer updates the dbuser_dual variables to Account B. On its next refresh ESO rewrites eso-shop-db-creds, the ESO Shop operator detects the change and performs a rolling restart (maxUnavailable: 0), and the new pods log in as appuser_02 while the old ones keep serving with Account A.
dual.s8_title: Grace Period Ends: CPM Changes Account A
dual.s8_desc: Only when the GracePeriod expires does CPM run the password change task for the inactive Account A: on MySQL and in the Vault. By then no consumer is using Account A, so the change is invisible to both paths.
dual.s9_title: Cycle Complete: Ready for the Next Rotation
dual.s9_desc: Both consumers run on Account B; Account A holds a fresh password and waits as Inactive. At the next rotation the roles reverse: B becomes Inactive, A becomes Active, and B's password is changed after the grace period.
dual.key4_desc: Two accounts with identical permissions, both enabled on the target, in the root of the same Safe, sharing a VirtualUserName that is unique in that Safe and grouped in one rotational group. Verify and reconcile run on the active account.

jwt.title: How JWT Authentication Works
jwt.subtitle: From pod startup to secret retrieval: a step-by-step animation of how workloads authenticate to Secrets Manager using Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWTs without any stored credentials.
jwt.s1_desc: Four actors in the JWT authentication flow: the Workload (app container in K8s), the K8s API Server (which issues and validates JWTs via its OIDC endpoint), the Secrets Manager JWT Authenticator (validates the token and resolves identity), and the Secrets Vault (stores and returns secret values).
jwt.s2_title: K8s Projects a JWT into the Pod
jwt.s2_desc: When the pod starts, Kubernetes automatically mounts a short-lived ServiceAccount JWT at /var/run/secrets/tokens/jwt. This token is signed by K8s and contains claims about the workload identity: sub (system:serviceaccount:conjur:springboot-app), namespace, serviceaccount name, iss (https://kubernetes.default.svc), and aud (conjur). No manual credential management.
jwt.s3_title: Workload POSTs JWT to Secrets Manager
jwt.s3_desc: The application reads the JWT from its projected volume and sends it to the authn-jwt endpoint: POST /api/authn-jwt/eks-latam/conjur/authenticate. The body contains only the URL-encoded JWT. No password, no API key: the workload's Kubernetes identity is the credential.
jwt.s4_title: Secrets Manager Fetches JWKS from K8s
jwt.s4_desc: Secrets Manager reads the jwks-uri policy variable (pointing to the K8s OIDC discovery URL). It fetches the JSON Web Key Set: the RSA public keys that K8s uses to sign ServiceAccount JWTs. If the signing key changes (K8s key rotation), Secrets Manager automatically fetches the new key when it encounters a token signed with it.
jwt.s5_desc: Using the fetched JWKS, Secrets Manager cryptographically verifies the JWT signature, confirming it was genuinely signed by this K8s cluster. It validates: exp (not expired), iss (matches configured issuer), aud (matches configured audience). A forged token, an expired token, or a token from a different cluster all fail here.
jwt.s6_desc: Secrets Manager extracts the claim specified in token-app-property (e.g. sub). It locates the matching host in policy (host/conjur/authn-jwt/eks-latam/springboot-app) and verifies ALL host annotations against the JWT claims: kubernetes/namespace-name: conjur ✓, kubernetes/service-account-name: springboot-app ✓. Every annotation is a mandatory constraint.
jwt.s7_desc: Authentication succeeds. Secrets Manager issues a short-lived API token: valid for approximately 8 minutes. This token proves the workload's authenticated identity to the Secrets Vault. The original K8s JWT is never stored or forwarded.
jwt.s8_desc: The workload uses the API token to fetch secrets: GET /api/secrets/conjur/variable/... with Authorization: Token token="<api-token>". Secrets Manager enforces policy entitlements. If authorized, the secret value is returned. No credential ever touches source code, a container image, or a CI variable.
jwt.key1_desc: The workload authenticates using its Kubernetes identity: a JWT projected by K8s itself. No API keys, no passwords, no certificates stored in the cluster. If the pod is compromised, there are no credentials to steal.
jwt.key2_desc: The JWT is signed by the Kubernetes API Server's RSA private key. Secrets Manager verifies this signature against the public JWKS before trusting any claims. Identity cannot be forged: only the real K8s cluster can produce a valid signature.
jwt.key3_desc: Every claim-to-identity mapping is declared in Secrets Manager policy YAML and version-controlled. Annotations on host resources define exactly which namespace, ServiceAccount, and pod labels are required. Change the policy to grant or revoke access: no credential rotation needed.

secretshub.title: How IDIRA Secrets Hub works
secretshub.subtitle: Secrets Hub is a SaaS service that keeps the secrets of your PAM solution (Privilege Cloud or PAM Self-Hosted) in sync with the stores developers already use: AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager and HashiCorp Vault. Developers keep the native APIs; security keeps rotation and audit in PAM.
secretshub.key1_desc: Applications keep reading from AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault with the same SDK calls. Secrets Hub only writes the value and its tags in the target store.
secretshub.key2_title: PAM stays the source of truth
secretshub.key2_desc: Secrets live in PAM Safes and the CPM rotates them by password policy. Secrets Hub syncs the new value to the targets continuously, so one audit trail and one rotation policy cover every cloud.
secretshub.key3_desc: Secrets Hub scans the target stores and shows every secret in one view, with insights such as unused secrets or secrets not rotated recently, so security can decide what to onboard to PAM.

env.hint_saas: Secrets come from Privilege Cloud, on the IDIRA Identity Security Platform.
env.hint_pamsh: Secrets come from your own PAM Self-Hosted Vault, reached through a connector in your data center.

saas.diagram_label: Secrets Hub with Privilege Cloud as the source
saas.s1_desc: Privilege Cloud holds the secrets and the CPM rotates them. Secrets Hub, a SaaS service on the IDIRA platform, syncs them to four kinds of target: AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager and HashiCorp Vault. Workloads read from the store they already use.
saas.s2_title: 2. The CPM rotates the secret in the Safe
saas.s2_desc: Each account in a Safe is a secret. The CPM (or SRS) rotates it according to the password policy, so PAM always has the current value.
saas.s3_title: 3. The SecretsHub user joins the Safe
saas.s3_desc: To sync a Safe, the SecretsHub user must be a Safe member with List and Retrieve accounts, Add account, Update account properties, View Safe members and Access Safe without confirmation. Permission changes can take up to 10 minutes to reach Secrets Hub.
saas.s4_title: 4. Trust with each cloud store, no stored keys
saas.s4_desc: AWS: an IAM role that Secrets Hub assumes (created by Connect cloud environments or by hand). Azure: an app registration with federated identity. GCP: Workload Identity Federation with a service account and a short-lived token.
saas.s5_desc: HashiCorp Vault always needs a connector, as do private AWS, Azure and GCP stores. The connector opens a long-lived outbound MQTT connection to Secrets Hub, so no inbound port is opened. Vault trusts Secrets Hub through a JWT/OIDC role.
saas.s6_desc: Secrets Hub discovers the secrets already in each target store and shows them in one view, with insights such as unused or not recently rotated secrets.
saas.s7_title: 7. A sync policy pushes the Safe to the targets
saas.s7_desc: A sync policy says which Safe goes to which target store. Secrets Hub writes each account as a secret tagged Sourced by CyberArk; for HashiCorp Vault the write goes through the connector.
saas.s8_desc: When the CPM rotates the account, Secrets Hub syncs the new value to every target. The sync is one way: manual edits in a target are not detected and can be overwritten, so restrict write access there.
saas.s9_desc: Applications keep their native calls: GetSecretValue in AWS, getSecret in Azure, accessSecretVersion in GCP and kv get in HashiCorp Vault. They receive the rotated value with no code change.

pamsh.diagram_label: Secrets Hub with PAM Self-Hosted as the source
pamsh.s1_desc: Your PAM Self-Hosted Vault holds the secrets and the CPM rotates them. Secrets Hub runs as SaaS, so a connector pool in your data center links it to PVWA. The same four kinds of target receive the secrets.
pamsh.s2_title: 2. The CPM rotates the secret in the Safe
pamsh.s2_desc: Each account in a Safe is a secret. The PAM Self-Hosted CPM rotates it according to the password policy.
pamsh.s3_title: 3. A connector pool links the data center to the cloud
pamsh.s3_desc: Install the connector (Connector Management agent on Windows) and set the PVWA URL, or its load balancer, in Secrets Hub. Traffic to the cloud uses TLS with an x509 client certificate (mTLS) and goes through your proxy if you have one.
pamsh.s4_desc: Create the SecretsHub user (type DAPService) in the Vault; Secrets Hub rotates its password. Add it as a member of each Safe to sync. The connector host must trust the PVWA certificate.
pamsh.s5_title: 5. Trust with each cloud store, no stored keys
pamsh.s5_desc: AWS: an IAM role that Secrets Hub assumes. Azure: an app registration with federated identity. GCP: Workload Identity Federation with a service account and a short-lived token.
pamsh.s6_desc: HashiCorp Vault always needs a connector, in the same network as the Vault. Use a separate pool from the one that reaches PAM. Vault trusts Secrets Hub through a JWT/OIDC role.
pamsh.s7_title: 7. Sync: through the connector to PVWA and out to the targets
pamsh.s7_desc: A sync policy says which Safe goes to which target. On each request the connector opens an ad hoc HTTPS connection to PVWA (local traffic, it bypasses the proxy), reads the account and Secrets Hub writes it to every target.
pamsh.s8_desc: When the CPM rotates the account, the new value takes the same path. The sync is one way: manual edits in a target are not detected and can be overwritten.
pamsh.s9_desc: Applications keep their native calls: GetSecretValue in AWS, getSecret in Azure, accessSecretVersion in GCP and kv get in HashiCorp Vault.

limits.title: Integration limitations and requirements
limits.sub: Read these before you design the rollout. They change with the PAM source you selected above.

general.title: General
items: Keys and certificates are not supported, only secrets. Dual accounts are not supported.
Up to 10,000 accounts synced per tenant and up to 1,000 sync policies.
Visibility: up to 150,000 secrets overall and 5,000 per secret store; up to 15,000 target secret stores.
One-way sync: manual changes in a target are not detected and can be overwritten. Restrict write access to synced secrets (for example, a deny policy in AWS).
Renaming an account in PAM creates a new secret in the target; the old one is not renamed or deleted. Deleting the account in PAM removes the target secret.
Up to 5 connectors per tenant. Connector host: Windows Server 2016 to 2025, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM, 500 MB disk.
Secrets Hub is supported in English only, because of character limits in the secret stores.

aws.title: AWS Secrets Manager
items: Secret names up to 512 characters.
Secrets Hub cannot change the value of secrets managed by AWS.
Stores created by Connect cloud environments are managed only there. Removing the organization deletes its stores, policies and synced secrets.

az.title: Azure Key Vault
items: Secret names up to 127 characters.
Key Vaults with the Access policy permission model are not supported: switch to RBAC.
Up to 2,000 Key Vaults per subscription. Key Vaults in different subscriptions behind a connector need network peering.
Onboarding a Microsoft Entra tenant uses federated identity only; client secret authentication is not supported.

gcp.title: GCP Secret Manager
items: Secret names up to 255 characters.
Labels are limited to 63 characters: long Safe or account names are truncated in the labels Secrets Hub adds.
The replication policy is set when the secret is created and cannot be changed later.

hcv.title: HashiCorp Vault
items: A connector is required for every HashiCorp Vault connection, in the same network as the Vault.
Only the Key/Value (KV) secrets engine version 2 is supported. Vault Community and Enterprise, version 1.2x.
Secret names up to 512 characters. Secrets Hub manages only secrets tagged Sourced by CyberArk.
Access is granted through a JWT/OIDC auth role and a Vault policy on the mount path (Terraform plan or bash script).

saas.title: Source: Privilege Cloud
items: Works with Privilege Cloud Standalone and Privilege Cloud Shared Services.
The SecretsHub user can be a member of up to 1,000 Safes; Safes with up to 1,000 accounts can be synced.
The connector table lists Privilege Cloud Vault as always requiring a connector; use a separate connector from the one for your cloud stores.

pamsh.title: Source: PAM Self-Hosted
items: PAM Self-Hosted version 11.5 or later.
A connector is always required to reach PAM Self-Hosted; use a connector pool for high availability.
Only one load balancer in front of PVWA is supported.
SecretsHub user: member of up to 1,000 Safes on version 12.1 and later, or 150 on 12.0 and earlier; up to 500 accounts per Safe.
The connector host must trust the PVWA TLS certificate. Connector to PVWA traffic bypasses the proxy; connector to the cloud goes through it.

jenkins.title: How Jenkins Fetches Secrets From IDIRA
jenkins.subtitle: The Secrets Manager Credentials Plugin lets Jenkins pipelines retrieve secrets from Secrets Manager at runtime using JWT authentication: no API keys stored in Jenkins, no credentials in Jenkinsfiles, no secrets in source code.
jenkins.s1_desc: Five components work together: the Jenkins Server running CI/CD pipelines with the Secrets Manager Credentials Plugin installed, the JWKS Endpoint exposed by Jenkins itself for JWT key verification, Secrets Manager with its JWT Authenticator webservice (authn-jwt/jenkins), and the Secrets Vault storing the actual secret values. No hardcoded credentials exist anywhere in this flow: not in Jenkinsfile, not in Jenkins config, not in environment.
jenkins.s2_desc: Two admins configure the integration once. The Jenkins admin installs the Secrets Manager Credentials Plugin (v3.x, requires Jenkins 2.455+), then in Manage Jenkins → System sets the Secrets Manager URL, account name, and JWT Auth Webservice ID (authn-jwt/jenkins). The Secrets Manager admin creates the JWT authenticator policy with variables: jwks-uri (pointing to Jenkins' JWKS endpoint), token-app-property (e.g. sub), issuer (Jenkins URL), audience (cyberark-conjur), then defines pipeline host identities with annotations (jenkins_pronoun: Pipeline, jenkins_full_name: Project1/pipeline) and grants them access to specific secret variables via !permit blocks.
jenkins.s3_desc: A developer pushes code to the repository or manually triggers a Jenkins build. The Jenkinsfile is committed to source control. It declares credentials via withCredentials([conjurSecretCredential(credentialsId: 'DB_PWD', variable: 'DB_PASSWORD')]). Only the Jenkins Credential ID appears in code. The actual secret path in Secrets Manager, the Secrets Manager URL, and the secret value are all absent from the Jenkinsfile. Security teams own the policy; developers own the pipeline.
jenkins.s4_title: withCredentials Activates the Plugin: JWT Generated
jenkins.s4_desc: When pipeline execution reaches the withCredentials block, the Secrets Manager Credentials Plugin activates. It generates a short-lived JWT (valid only 2 minutes) signed by Jenkins' own RSA private key. The JWT contains: iss (Jenkins URL), aud (cyberark-conjur), sub (the pipeline's jenkins_full_name, e.g. Project1/pipeline), and exp (now + 120 seconds). This JWT is the pipeline's identity credential: there is no API key to store, rotate, or leak. The identity is structural: the job path in Jenkins IS the credential.
jenkins.s5_desc: The plugin POSTs the JWT to Secrets Manager's authn-jwt/jenkins endpoint. Secrets Manager reads its jwks-uri policy variable and fetches the JSON Web Key Set from Jenkins' JWKS endpoint (https://jenkins/jwtauth/conjur-jwk-set). Using the returned RSA public key it cryptographically verifies the JWT signature, confirming the token was genuinely issued by this Jenkins instance. Standard claims are then validated: exp (not expired), iss (matches configured issuer), aud (matches cyberark-conjur).
jenkins.s6_desc: Secrets Manager extracts the sub claim (Project1/pipeline) and maps it via token-app-property to a host in policy. It verifies all host annotations match JWT claims: jenkins_full_name: Project1/pipeline ✓, jenkins_pronoun: Pipeline ✓. Then it checks the !permit block: does this host have read/execute privilege on the requested variable paths? If all pass, a short-lived Secrets Manager API token is issued and the secrets are fetched from the Vault. Each variable access is logged for audit.
jenkins.s7_title: Secrets Returned and Injected as Environment Variables
jenkins.s7_desc: Secrets Manager returns the secret values to the plugin over HTTPS. The plugin injects each value into the build environment under the variable name specified in the Jenkinsfile (DB_PASSWORD, API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN, etc.). Values exist only in memory for the duration of the withCredentials block scope. They are never written to disk, never appear in build artifacts, and are never stored in Jenkins' credential store in plaintext.
jenkins.s8_title: Pipeline Executes: All Secrets Auto-Masked in Logs
jenkins.s8_desc: The pipeline steps inside withCredentials execute with real secret values available as environment variables. Shell commands, deployment scripts, and test suites use $DB_PASSWORD, $API_KEY normally. Jenkins automatically intercepts all log output and replaces every occurrence of a secret value with ***. Even if a developer accidentally echoes a variable, the log shows ***. When the withCredentials block exits, all values are cleared from memory. The build succeeds with no trace of any credential in logs, artifacts, or source code.
jenkins.key1_desc: No API keys, passwords, or secret paths appear in Jenkinsfile or Jenkins configuration. Pipeline code references only Jenkins Credential IDs (like 'DB_PWD'). Security teams control the Secrets Manager policy and secret paths independently of developers: no coordination needed to rotate.
jenkins.key2_desc: Each build authenticates using a 2-minute JWT signed by Jenkins itself. No stored API key, no long-lived credential, nothing to rotate for the Jenkins identity. If a token is intercepted it expires before it can be reused. The job path in Jenkins (Project1/pipeline) is the identity.
jenkins.key3_desc: Jenkins automatically masks all secret values in build logs. The withCredentials block is the scope boundary: secrets are available only within it and cleared on exit. Three credential tiers (Global, Folder, Job) allow shared secrets across teams with inheritance control via jenkins_pronoun annotations.
jenkins.arch1_desc: Installed via Jenkins Plugin Manager. Bridges Jenkins Credential Store with Secrets Manager. Supports JWT (keyless, recommended) and API key auth. Works with Declarative and Scripted Pipelines, and Freestyle projects.
jenkins.arch2_desc: Jenkins acts as its own OIDC token issuer. Each build generates a scoped JWT signed by Jenkins' private key. Secrets Manager verifies the signature against the public JWKS endpoint. No secret is stored in Jenkins to enable auth.
jenkins.arch3_desc: Three tiers: Global (visible to all jobs), Folder (shared within a folder, inherited by subfolders), Job/Pipeline (job-specific). Each tier maps to a Secrets Manager host with annotation jenkins_pronoun: Global | Folder | Pipeline.
jenkins.arch4_desc: Secrets Manager policy !permit blocks define exactly which pipeline host identities can read which secret variables. Changing access (grant or revoke) is a policy update: no secret rotation, no credential redistribution, immediate effect.

ansible.title: How Ansible Fetches Secrets From IDIRA
ansible.subtitle: The cyberark.conjur collection's lookup plugin lets Ansible playbooks retrieve secrets from Secrets Manager at run time, authenticated with a JWT from your IdP. No API keys in inventory, no credentials in playbooks, no secrets on managed nodes.
ansible.s1_desc: Five components work together: the Ansible Control Node running the playbook with the cyberark.conjur collection and its lookup plugin installed; the IdP / JWKS Endpoint that issues the JWT and exposes the public keys; Secrets Manager SaaS with its JWT Authenticator webservice (authn-jwt/ansible); and the Secrets Vault holding the actual values. No hardcoded credential exists anywhere: not in the playbook, not in inventory, not in host_vars.
ansible.s2_desc: Install the collection on the control node (ansible-galaxy collection install cyberark.conjur). The Secrets Manager admin creates the JWT authenticator policy (authn-jwt/ansible) with the variables jwks-uri (pointing at the IdP's JWKS), token-app-property, issuer and audience (cyberark-conjur), defines an ansible host identity and grants it read/execute on the secret variables via !permit. The operator supplies the connection via extra-vars or environment variables (CONJUR_APPLIANCE_URL, CONJUR_AUTHN_LOGIN, CONJUR_AUTHN_TYPE=jwt, CONJUR_AUTHN_SERVICE_ID).
ansible.s3_desc: The operator runs ansible-playbook retrieve-secrets.yaml. The playbook is committed to source control. It references secrets only through the Jinja2 lookup {{ lookup('cyberark.conjur.conjur_variable', 'data/ansible/db-password') }}: only the secret ID appears in the YAML. The Secrets Manager URL, host identity and the actual value are supplied out-of-band (env / extra-vars) and never live in the playbook.
ansible.s4_desc: When a task hits the conjur_variable lookup, the plugin runs on the control node. With authn_type=jwt it uses a JWT obtained from your Identity Provider: typically a prior task fetches and saves the JWT from the IdP. The token carries iss (IdP), aud (cyberark-conjur) and sub (the ansible host identity). There is no static API key to store or rotate: the JWT is the control node's short-lived identity credential.
ansible.s5_desc: The plugin POSTs the JWT to Secrets Manager's authn-jwt/ansible endpoint. Secrets Manager reads its jwks-uri policy variable and fetches the JSON Web Key Set from the IdP. Using the public key it cryptographically verifies the JWT signature, then validates the standard claims: exp (not expired), iss (matches the configured issuer) and aud (matches cyberark-conjur).
ansible.s6_desc: Secrets Manager maps the sub claim via token-app-property to a host in policy and confirms the annotations match. It then checks the !permit block: does this ansible host have read/execute on the requested variable path? If so, a short-lived Secrets Manager access token is issued and the secret is read from the Vault. Every access is logged for audit.
ansible.s7_title: Secret Returned and Bound to an Ansible Variable
ansible.s7_desc: Secrets Manager returns the value to the plugin over HTTPS. The lookup resolves to the plaintext value inside the play: bound to an Ansible variable or used directly in a task (template, copy, uri, etc.). The value lives only in the control node's memory for the play; it is never written to inventory, host_vars or disk.
ansible.s8_title: Task Runs on Managed Nodes: Value Kept Off Logs
ansible.s8_desc: Tasks apply the secret to the managed nodes (render a config template, set a DB password, deploy a key). Mark the task with no_log: true so Ansible never prints the value in output or -v logs; the PLAY RECAP shows success with the value masked. When the play ends the value is cleared from memory: no credential remains in the playbook, in inventory or on the managed hosts.
ansible.key1_desc: Playbooks reference only Secrets Manager secret IDs via lookup(). No passwords, keys or vault paths live in YAML, inventory or host_vars. Security teams own the policy and secret paths independently of the automation authors: no coordination needed to rotate.
ansible.key2_desc: The lookup plugin supports API key, AWS IAM, Azure Managed Identity, GCP and JWT authentication. With JWT the control node authenticates using a short-lived token from your IdP, nothing static to store or rotate. If a token is intercepted it expires before it can be reused.
ansible.key3_desc: Secrets are fetched at play execution and exist only in the control node's memory for that run. Combined with no_log they never appear in logs or artifacts. Optionally the conjur_host_identity role installs Summon to keep secrets off disk on managed nodes.
ansible.arch1_desc: Installed from Ansible Galaxy (ansible-galaxy collection install cyberark.conjur). Provides the conjur_variable lookup plugin and the conjur_host_identity role. Works with any playbook: the lookup path requires no changes on the managed nodes.
ansible.arch2_desc: The control node sends a JWT from your IdP to the authn-jwt/ansible webservice. Secrets Manager verifies the signature against the IdP's public JWKS. No API key is stored on the control node to enable authentication.
ansible.arch3_desc: The conjur_host_identity role enrolls managed nodes with a Conjur identity (via a Host Factory token) and installs Summon, so applications on those hosts can fetch secrets and keep them off disk, injected as environment variables at start.
ansible.arch4_desc: Secrets Manager policy !permit blocks define exactly which host identities can read which secret variables. Granting or revoking access is a policy update: no secret rotation, no credential redistribution, immediate effect.

csi.title: How the Secrets Store CSI Driver Delivers Secrets
csi.subtitle: A demo pod consumes the dbuser_dual secret from CyberArk Conjur Cloud through the Secrets Store CSI Driver (Conjur provider). The values are mounted into the pod as a read-only tmpfs volume (no Kubernetes Secret, no API key, no secret in the image) and the driver re-fetches them every 2 minutes.
csi.s1_desc: The demo runs in the EKS your-cluster cluster (namespace conjur). Five parts work together: the pod csidriver-app (a small Python app plus a CSI-mounted tmpfs volume), the Secrets Store CSI Driver and the conjur-k8s-csi-provider (both DaemonSets in kube-system), and CyberArk Conjur Cloud (tenant your-tenant) holding the dbuser_dual secret behind the authn-jwt/your-cluster authenticator. No secret value is stored in a Kubernetes Secret, in the image, or in Git.
csi.s2_desc: A SecretProviderClass (csidriver-secrets) declares the Conjur connection (applianceUrl, account, authnId (authn-jwt/your-cluster) and the CA chain) with no secretObjects, so delivery is volume-only. The pod carries a conjur.org/secrets annotation mapping each file (username.txt, password.txt, address.txt) to a Conjur variable path, exposed to the provider through a downwardAPI podinfo volume. A dedicated ServiceAccount (csidriver) is the workload identity, and on the Conjur side a matching workload with read/execute on dbuser_dual is authorized.
csi.s3_desc: A request to demo.minha.cloud/csidriver enters through the nginx-internal ingress (TLS), which rewrites the path and forwards it to csidriver-service (ClusterIP 80 → 8080). The Python app handles the request and, on every load, reads the three files under /mnt/conjur-csi-volume. Nothing about the secret lives in the app code: only the mount path.
csi.s4_desc: When the pod starts, the kubelet asks the Secrets Store CSI Driver to mount the volume (NodePublishVolume). The driver requests a projected ServiceAccount token for the csidriver SA with audience conjur (as declared in the CSIDriver tokenRequests) and hands it, together with the pod's conjur.org/secrets mapping, to the conjur-k8s-csi-provider running on the same node.
csi.s5_desc: The Conjur provider presents the projected token as a JWT to the authn-jwt/your-cluster authenticator on Conjur Cloud. Conjur cryptographically verifies the token against the cluster's public keys and validates the claims: the sub is system:serviceaccount:conjur:csidriver, the audience is conjur. This is keyless workload identity: there is no API key stored on the node or in the pod.
csi.s6_desc: Conjur maps the authenticated identity to a workload and checks its permissions: does system:serviceaccount:conjur:csidriver have read/execute on data/vault/demo-safe/dbuser_dual/{username,password,address}? If so, the values are read from the Vault. A successful mount is itself the proof that the workload and permissions on the Conjur side are correct: otherwise the pod would stay in ContainerCreating.
csi.s7_title: Secrets Written to the tmpfs Volume
csi.s7_desc: The provider returns the values to the driver, which writes each one to its file under /mnt/conjur-csi-volume (username.txt, password.txt, address.txt) on a tmpfs, read-only volume. The values live only in the node's memory for the pod: never persisted to disk, never written to a Kubernetes Secret, and never leaving the volume.
csi.s8_title: App Serves the Values: Automatic Rotation
csi.s8_desc: The app reads the files on each request and renders the values (password masked; ?reveal=1 shows it). The driver's rotation reconciler polls Conjur every 2 minutes (rotationPollInterval 2m0s, enable-secret-rotation=true) and rewrites the files if dbuser_dual changed. The page auto-refreshes every 5 seconds, so a rotation appears within ~2 minutes: with no pod restart and no redeploy.
csi.key1_desc: Secrets are delivered straight into a read-only tmpfs volume in the pod: never materialized as a Kubernetes Secret object and never baked into the image. The app knows only the mount path (/mnt/conjur-csi-volume); the value exists solely in the node's memory.
csi.key2_desc: The pod authenticates with a short-lived projected ServiceAccount token (audience conjur) verified by authn-jwt/your-cluster. Nothing static is stored: no API key on the node or in the pod. The identity is the ServiceAccount itself (sub=system:serviceaccount:conjur:csidriver).
csi.key3_desc: The driver's rotation reconciler re-fetches from Conjur every 2 minutes and rewrites the volume in place: no pod restart. requiresRepublish is false because the reconciler, not the kubelet, drives updates. Changing the interval affects every CSI-mounted app on the cluster.
csi.config_note: Live values from the cluster (verified 2026-07-19), passed as environment variables to the pod.
csi.arch1_desc: A DaemonSet in kube-system implementing the secrets-store.csi.k8s.io interface. It mounts secret material as an ephemeral (tmpfs) volume and runs the rotation reconciler, delegating the actual secret fetch to a provider.
csi.arch2_desc: A DaemonSet (also kube-system) that the driver calls over gRPC. It reads the pod's conjur.org/secrets mapping, authenticates to Conjur with the projected ServiceAccount JWT, and returns the requested variable values.
csi.arch3_desc: The namespaced object (csidriver-secrets) that declares the Conjur connection: applianceUrl, account, authnId and CA chain. Here it has no secretObjects, so secrets are delivered only into the volume, not synced to a Kubernetes Secret.
csi.arch4_desc: The driver control loop that polls the provider on rotation-poll-interval (2m) when enable-secret-rotation is true, rewriting the volume when the source changes. It is the update path here, since CSIDriver.requiresRepublish is false.

policy.title: How Secrets Manager Policy is Structured
policy.subtitle: Secrets Manager policy is YAML loaded into a tree of branches. Each !policy statement creates a namespace, resources inside get fully-qualified IDs, and roles + permits drive every authorization decision. This animation walks through the structure one concept at a time.
policy.s1_title: Policy as a Tree of Branches
policy.s1_desc: Secrets Manager policy is plain YAML: a list of statements. When loaded, those statements build a tree of branches rooted at a single implicit container: the account itself. Every secret, every identity and every authorization rule lives somewhere on this tree, addressable by its path. The animation will progressively introduce each piece: the root, branches created by !policy, the resources inside them, and how !permit and !grant tie identities to secrets.
policy.s2_desc: A !policy statement at the top of the file creates a top-level branch under the root. It has three keys: id (its name, e.g. prod), owner (a role that controls the branch: usually a group like prod-admins), and body (the list of statements that live inside it). The owner has full authority over everything declared inside the branch and is the only role that can replace or delete its contents.
policy.s3_desc: Branches nest arbitrarily. A !policy declared inside another !policy's body creates a sub-branch. Here, app1 is a sub-branch of prod. Nesting is how teams partition ownership: prod is owned by prod-admins, while app1 can declare its own owner so that the app1 team manages its own resources without touching the rest of prod.
policy.s4_desc: Every resource declared inside a branch is namespaced by it. The !variable db-password declared inside prod/app1 is referenced everywhere as prod/app1/db-password. Two branches can declare the same local name without colliding: they live in different namespaces. The fully-qualified ID is what tools, APIs and audit logs always use.
policy.s5_desc: Roles are anything that can act. !host is a machine identity (a workload, pipeline, server), !user is a person, !group bundles roles together for delegation, and !layer groups hosts. Roles, like resources, get fully-qualified IDs. The !group admins declared inside prod/app1 is prod/app1/admins: that exact identifier is what !permit and !grant refer to.
policy.s6_desc: !permit attaches privileges to a (role, resource) pair. Here, the admins group is permitted read and execute on db-password, meaning anyone in that group can fetch its value. The privilege set is fixed per resource type: variables support read, execute, update; policies support read, create, update, delete. !permit is additive: multiple permits on the same resource simply union the privileges.
policy.s7_desc: !grant adds a member role to a parent role. Granting app1-host membership in admins means app1-host inherits every privilege admins ever had, including the read/execute on db-password from the previous step. This is how indirection works: hosts and users are added to groups; groups are what permits target. To revoke access, change the grant: never touch the permit. Groups can grant into groups; layers can grant into layers; the hierarchy can be as deep as you need.
policy.s8_desc: Putting it all together: branches partition the namespace and ownership, resources live inside branches with fully-qualified IDs, roles identify who can act, !permit names what they can do on each resource, and !grant binds identities into the role hierarchy. Loading this YAML produces exactly the tree on the right, addressable by paths like prod/app1/db-password. Editing the YAML and re-loading is the only way state ever changes: policy is the single source of truth.
policy.key1_desc: Every !policy creates a branch. Resources inside it are addressed as branch/sub-branch/resource. Branches partition ownership: one team can manage prod/app1 without touching prod/app2. Nesting is unbounded: design the tree to match your org.
policy.key2_desc: Roles (!host, !user, !group, !layer) are anything that acts. Resources (!variable, !webservice, !policy) are anything acted upon. !permit connects them with a privilege set, !grant inserts roles into the role hierarchy. Every authorization is computed from this graph.
policy.key3_desc: Policy is plain YAML committed to git. Loading is the only mutation: replace mode overwrites a branch, patch mode adds and removes specific items, update mode adds without deleting. Pull requests review every change to identity and access: auditable, reversible, version-controlled.

secret.title: What is a secret?
secret.def: A secret is a credential that grants access to something valuable: database passwords, API keys, TLS certificates and keys, SSH keys, cloud credentials. Whoever holds it can use it: so it must never live in code, container images or config files.
points: Stored encrypted as a variable; every access is controlled and audited.
Each secret has two access lists: fetchers (who can read it) and updaters (who can change it).
Static, dynamic (just-in-time and short-lived) or synced every minute from PAM, where the CPM rotates it.

identity.title: What is a machine identity?
identity.def: A machine (workload) identity is how a non-human actor (an app, container, CI job, script, playbook or VM) proves who it is. It is not a password the workload keeps: it is evidence its platform already issues and IDIRA can verify.
points: Represented in policy as a host, with only the privileges its job needs.
Proves itself to an authenticator (authn-jwt, authn-iam, OIDC) and receives a short-lived access token.
Best practice: one identity per workload element. Not one shared identity for a whole cluster or CI server.

prove.title: Prove
prove.desc: The workload presents its identity: for example its Kubernetes ServiceAccount JWT.

authorize.title: Authorize
authorize.desc: Policy checks that this host is a fetcher of the secret it asks for.

deliver.title: Deliver
deliver.desc: The secret arrives at run time, rotated and audited, never stored with the workload.

fundamentals.zero_desc: The identity replaces the bootstrap password, so a workload never needs a secret to get its secrets.

flowlive.title: Identity first, every time
flowlive.subtitle: Follow two workloads to their service: one fetches a secret using its identity, the other needs no secret at all.

practice.title: Secret or identity?
practice.subtitle: They are often confused, and the difference is the whole point: a secret is what you protect; an identity is how a workload earns access to it.

issuer.identity: The platform the workload runs on: Kubernetes, GitHub, Jenkins, AWS or a SPIFFE server

lifetime.secret: Long-lived if static; short-lived if dynamic or rotated by CPM
lifetime.identity: Short-lived and renewed automatically by the platform

leak.secret: Grants access to the target until it is rotated or revoked

metaphor.label: Secret vs identity, in everyday terms
metaphor.secret_title: A secret is a key that opens a door
metaphor.secret_desc: Whoever holds the key gets in. The door does not know who you are, only that the key fits. If someone copies it, the copy opens the door too, until the lock is changed (rotation).
metaphor.identity_title: An identity is a passport someone attested
metaphor.identity_desc: It proves who you are, and it only counts because a trusted issuer attested it: Kubernetes, GitHub, AWS or a SPIFFE server. It expires quickly, and the border (IDIRA) checks the issuer before letting you through.

glossary.title: The vocabulary, in one place
glossary.subtitle: Terms used across this site, as the Secrets Manager docs define them.

workload.def: A non-human actor: application, container, CI job, script, playbook, VM or service.

host.def: How a workload identity is represented in Secrets Manager policy: with only the privileges its job needs.

authenticator.def: The Secrets Manager service that verifies an identity’s evidence (authn-jwt, authn-iam, OIDC…) before any secret is released.

token.def: Short-lived token returned after a successful authentication; the workload uses it to fetch the secrets it may read.

policy.def: Declarative YAML that defines identities, secrets and permissions: kept in git and reviewed like code.

variable.def: The record that stores a secret in Secrets Manager. PAM accounts sync in as data/vault/<safe>/<account>/<property>.

fetchers.def: The two access lists of every secret: who may read it and who may change it.

dynamic.def: Created just-in-time for one consumer and valid for a short period, then deleted or obsolete.

rotation.def: Changing a credential on a schedule. In PAM the CPM rotates it, and Secrets Manager syncs the new value every minute.

secretzero.def: The first credential a workload would need in order to fetch all the others. Identity-based authentication removes it.

spiffe.def: Open standard for workload identity; the SVID (X.509 or JWT) is the document a workload presents. Used by Secure Workload Access.

nhi.def: Umbrella term for identities that are not people: workloads, service accounts, certificates, API keys. Machine identity is how workloads prove who they are.

idflow.diagram_label: Two ways a workload reaches a service
idflow.lane_a: Path 1 · identity, then secret, then service
idflow.lane_b: Path 2 · identity straight to the service
idflow.s1_title: Two ways to reach a service
idflow.s1_desc: On top, an application uses its identity to fetch a secret and then reach the database. Below, a workload uses only its identity to reach the service, with no secret at all. Step through it or press play.
idflow.s2_desc: When the pod starts, Kubernetes projects a ServiceAccount JWT into it. The application stores no password: this token is its identity.
idflow.s3_desc: The application sends the JWT to the authn-jwt authenticator of IDIRA Secrets Manager, which checks the signature (JWKS), the issuer and the claims, and maps the workload to a host in policy.
idflow.s4_desc: With the identity proven, Secrets Manager returns a short-lived access token. That token, not a password, authorizes the next calls.
idflow.s5_desc: The application asks for the variable with its access token. Policy checks that this host is a fetcher of the secret, and the vault returns the database password at run time.
idflow.s6_desc: With the secret in memory, the application connects to MySQL. Nothing is left in code, images or config files, and the password can be rotated by the CPM.
idflow.s7_desc: On the second path, the Secure Workload Access agent attests the workload (node and pod) and issues an SVID: its SPIFFE identity, short-lived and renewed automatically.
idflow.s8_title: 7. The workload presents the SVID to AWS
idflow.s8_desc: The workload sends its JWT-SVID to AWS STS (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity). AWS validates the token against the trust bundle published by the SWA trust domain.
idflow.s9_desc: STS returns temporary credentials for the federated role. They expire on their own and never need to be stored or rotated.
idflow.s10_desc: With those credentials the workload reads the S3 bucket. No secret was created, stored or distributed: the identity was the only credential.
idflow.s11_desc: Path 1: the identity fetches the secret just in time, and the secret never lives in the workload. Path 2: the identity is the credential, and there is no secret. In both, identity decides access.

sharch.title: Secrets Manager Self‑Hosted architecture
sharch.subtitle: How a high availability IDIRA Secrets Manager Self-Hosted deployment is built: one Leader that writes, Standbys ready to take over, and Followers that serve reads close to the applications.
sharch.diagram_label: IDIRA Secrets Manager Self-Hosted architecture: Leader, Standbys, DR Standby, Followers, load balancers, Vault Synchronizer, KMS or HSM and SIEM
sharch.lane_primary: Primary region · AZ a / AZ b
sharch.s1_desc: Only the Leader accepts writes. Followers are read-only copies that answer the applications. Everything else in the picture exists to keep these two roles available and in sync.
sharch.s2_title: 2. Policies are loaded on the Leader
sharch.s2_desc: An administrator or a CI pipeline loads policy through the cluster load balancer on port 443. The load balancer only sends traffic to the active Leader, the node that answers its health check.
sharch.s3_desc: Vault Synchronizer syncs accounts from PAM Self-Hosted Safes to Secrets Manager. You add its Line of Business user to a Safe and each account becomes secrets: one for the password and one per synced property.
sharch.s4_desc: Standbys copy the Leader database with PostgreSQL streaming replication on port 5432. A write is only complete when the synchronous Standby also has it, so it is always up to date. Asynchronous Standbys catch up with eventual consistency.
sharch.s5_title: 5. A DR Standby in another region
sharch.s5_desc: The DR Standby replicates asynchronously in a site outside the auto-failover cluster. If the whole primary region is lost, it can be promoted to Leader manually.
sharch.s6_title: 6. Followers replicate through the cluster LB
sharch.s6_desc: Followers replicate from the Leader on port 5432, always through the cluster load balancer. That way they reach whichever node is the healthy Leader, without being reconfigured after a failover.
sharch.s7_title: 7. Workloads read from a nearby Follower
sharch.s7_desc: The workload calls the Follower load balancer on port 443. A Follower authenticates it, checks its permissions and returns the secret with low latency. Write operations against a Follower fail with an error.
sharch.s8_title: 8. Audit flows back to the Leader
sharch.s8_desc: Followers stream their audit events to the Leader on port 1999. The Leader keeps audit locally (audit.json, audit.log and the audit database) and does not replicate it, so export it to a SIEM.
sharch.s9_title: 9. Server keys protected by a master key
sharch.s9_desc: By default the server keys are stored on the node in cleartext. The recommendation is to encrypt them with a master key kept in AWS KMS or in a hardware security module (HSM).
sharch.s10_desc: The Leader and Standbys share their health with etcd. If the Leader stays unavailable beyond its TTL, Raft elects the most up-to-date Standby as the new Leader. The load balancer health check (port 444) now routes to it and Followers rebase automatically.
sharch.s11_desc: If the primary region becomes unavailable, promote the DR Standby to Leader manually. DR Standbys and Followers rebase through the cluster load balancer, which finds the healthy Leader for them.
sharch.components_sub: Every node is a Secrets Manager container (Docker or Podman). Followers can also run as Pods in Kubernetes or OpenShift.
sharch.c_leader_desc: The single active node that performs read and write operations. Policies and secrets are updated here.
sharch.c_sync_desc: Inactive replica that confirms every transaction together with the Leader, so it is always up to date. There can be only one.
sharch.c_async_desc: Inactive replica in eventual consistency mode; it may lag behind the Leader depending on load and size of changes.
sharch.c_dr_desc: Standby in a site outside the auto-failover cluster. It can only be promoted to Leader manually.
sharch.c_raft_desc: In an auto-failover cluster, nodes share health through etcd. When the Leader TTL expires, Raft selects the most up-to-date Standby as Leader.
sharch.c_follower_desc: Read-only replica close to the applications. Handles authentication, permission checks and secret fetches, and keeps serving if the Leader is temporarily unhealthy.
sharch.c_k8sfollower_desc: A Follower defined as a Kubernetes API resource and deployed by an Operator, running as microservices inside the cluster.
sharch.c_clb_desc: Well known endpoint that forwards requests to the active Leader only, based on the /health check. Followers and DR Standbys connect through it.
sharch.c_flb_desc: Spreads API requests across two or more Followers in the same location.
sharch.c_vsync_desc: Syncs accounts from PAM Self-Hosted Safes to Secrets Manager through a Line of Business user added to each Safe.
sharch.c_kms_desc: Holds the master key that encrypts the server keys at rest.
sharch.c_siem_desc: Receives the audit exported from the Leader, which keeps it locally and does not replicate it.
sharch.ports_sub: From the Accessibility section of the architecture reference.
sharch.port_443: TLS endpoint for the Secrets Manager UI and API, reached from the load balancer.
sharch.port_444: HTTP health endpoint that simplifies the load balancer setup.
sharch.port_1999: Audit events streamed from the Followers to the Leader (syslog-ng), through the load balancer.
sharch.port_5432: PostgreSQL data replication from the Leader to Standbys and Followers.
sharch.port_22: SSH for setup and management. Not required by Secrets Manager (optional on Followers); any port can be used.
sharch.lb_sub: The cluster load balancer finds the Leader; the Follower load balancer spreads reads.
sharch.lb_cluster_desc: Gives the cluster a well known endpoint and forwards requests to the active Leader. It must:
lb_cluster_items: Preserve the source IP address, for IP restrictions and audit.
Pass TLS through instead of terminating it: Follower to Leader traffic and Kubernetes authentication use mutual TLS.
Override the health check port and protocol and query the /health endpoint for all routes.
Forward traffic to the active Leader only: it is the only node that answers 200 OK to the health check.
sharch.lb_follower_desc: Balances API requests over two or more Followers in the same location. When required, it should:
lb_follower_items: Keep the source IP address, or add an X-Forwarded-For header with the original client IP.
Pass TLS through for mutual TLS, without terminating it.
With non-transparent proxies, the first one is a layer 7 proxy, all are listed as trusted proxies and clients cannot bypass it.
bp_items: Use multiple regions and availability zones, so a failing region or AZ does not affect availability.
Keep an odd number of nodes in the auto-failover cluster: 1 Leader and 2 or 4 Standbys, plus any number of DR Standbys.
Run the Leader and the synchronous Standby in the same region but in different AZs.
Put asynchronous Standbys in another AZ, or in the synchronous Standby AZ, so a quorum remains if the Leader AZ fails.
Run asynchronous DR Standbys in a different region from the cluster.
Run Followers as close as possible to the applications they serve, behind a load balancer.
Encrypt the server keys with a master key in AWS KMS or an HSM, and export the Leader audit to a SIEM.

roles.leader_desc: All writes (policies and secrets) go to the single active Leader. It is the only node that accepts changes.
roles.standby_desc: At least two Standbys replicate the Leader with PostgreSQL streaming replication; one is promoted if the Leader fails.
roles.follower_desc: Read-only replicas close to the workloads handle authentication, permission checks and secret fetches at scale.

saasarch.title: Secrets Manager SaaS architecture
saasarch.subtitle: How IDIRA Secrets Manager SaaS is laid out: the platform services in the Idira cloud, the PAM sources that feed it, and the Edges that serve secrets inside your own network, even offline.

benefits.readonly_desc: Edge gives workloads read-only access to secrets without opening inbound firewall rules from the external servers to your network.
benefits.ha_desc: Edge keeps serving secrets if connectivity to the SaaS or to the AWS region is lost, and survives a restart thanks to its persistent cache.
benefits.latency_desc: Edge runs next to your workloads, so authentication and secret reads stay local and each Edge handles up to 150 requests per second.

saasarch.flow_intro: The SaaS tenant lives on the Idira Shared Services platform (ISPSS). Secrets come from Privilege Cloud or from PAM Self-Hosted, and are replicated to Edges that you run behind a load balancer. Workloads use the nearby Edge or call the SaaS directly.

flow.diagram_label: Secrets Manager SaaS reference architecture with Edges
flow.s1_desc: Secrets Manager SaaS is a service on the Idira Shared Services platform, next to Identity and Privilege Cloud. Inside your network you run Edges, close to the workloads.
flow.s2_desc: Administrators reach the SaaS console with the platform shared services: user management, SSO and MFA, with audit kept centrally.
flow.s3_desc: Add the Conjur Sync user to a Safe and each account becomes secrets in Secrets Manager, one per property, plus a group with read and execute. When CPM rotates the password, the new value syncs in near real time.
flow.s4_desc: With PAM Self-Hosted, the Vault Synchronizer syncs the Safes that have the ConjurSync LOB user as a member. It authenticates with an API key and encrypts data in transit with an x509 client certificate (mTLS).
flow.s5_desc: Each Edge opens an outbound 443 connection to the tenant, optionally through an explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxy, and replicates secrets and workloads. Nothing on the internet needs to reach the Edge.
flow.s6_desc: The firewall rules also allow outbound 443 to an AWS IoT endpoint in the same region. New and updated secrets and workloads reach the Edges almost immediately; other resources, such as groups, within a few minutes.
flow.s7_desc: A workload calls the load balancer, which picks a healthy Edge. The Edge authenticates it locally (API key, JWT, GCP, client certificate or Azure) and returns the secret with low latency.
flow.s8_desc: Authentication and secret retrieval stay on the Edge. Dynamic secret requests, certificate requests and every other action are forwarded to Secrets Manager SaaS.
flow.s9_desc: If the link to the SaaS or the AWS region drops, the Edges keep serving secrets from their persistent cache, even after a container restart during the outage.
flow.s10_desc: Each Edge writes audit events (authentication and secret retrieval) to audit.json and service events to edge.log in its persistence folder. A SIEM agent on the host, such as the Splunk Universal Forwarder, ships them.
flow.s11_desc: Workloads authenticate and fetch secrets from their nearby Edge or straight from Secrets Manager SaaS. A cloud workload with internet access can call the tenant directly.

secretflow.diagram_label: An application with a hardcoded, static secret
secretflow.s1_desc: A secret is anything that grants access: a database password, an API key, a token, the private key of a certificate. Here, the password of the orders database is the secret.
secretflow.s2_title: 2. The password is typed into the code
secretflow.s2_desc: To make it work quickly, the developer writes the password in a config file. This is a hardcoded, static secret, and it is the root of the problem.
secretflow.s3_title: 3. Commit: the secret is in git forever
secretflow.s3_desc: After the commit, the password lives in the repository history. Deleting the line later does not remove it: every clone and fork keeps a copy.
secretflow.s4_title: 4. Build: the secret is inside the image
secretflow.s4_desc: CI builds the container image with the config file in it. Anyone who can pull the image can read the password.
secretflow.s5_desc: The app reads the password from its own files and connects to the database. Nothing looks wrong, which is why hardcoded secrets survive for years.
secretflow.s6_title: 6. The problem: whoever has a copy gets in
secretflow.s6_desc: A clone of the repo, a pulled image, a backup or a log is enough. The database cannot tell the real app from someone using the same password.
secretflow.s7_title: 7. Rotating it means a new release
secretflow.s7_desc: To change the password you edit the code, rebuild and redeploy, and every old copy stays valid until you do. So in practice it never changes.
secretflow.s8_title: 8. The fix: no secret in the code
secretflow.s8_desc: Store the secret in a vault and let the app fetch it at runtime, proving who it is with its own identity. The next concepts show how.

idconcept.diagram_label: How a workload proves who it is with a machine identity
idconcept.n_thief_sub: an old token from a log
idconcept.s1_desc: It is how a workload (an app, a pod, a pipeline job) proves who it is, like a passport. The workload does not carry a password: its identity comes from the platform where it runs.
idconcept.s2_title: 2. The platform issues and signs it
idconcept.s2_desc: Kubernetes knows exactly which pod this is, so it hands the pod a short-lived token signed with the platform private key: namespace orders, ServiceAccount api, valid for 10 minutes.
idconcept.s3_desc: When it needs something, the workload shows that token to IDIRA. It is like showing a passport at the border: no password involved.
idconcept.s4_desc: IDIRA fetches the issuer public keys and verifies the signature. Only identities signed by a platform you trust are accepted.
idconcept.s5_title: 5. IDIRA checks the claims against policy
idconcept.s5_desc: The token says who the workload is (namespace, ServiceAccount, repository, role). IDIRA compares that with the policy to decide what this specific workload may access.
idconcept.s6_desc: IDIRA returns short-lived access (a token or the secret the policy allows), and the workload connects to the service.
idconcept.s7_title: 7. It expires and renews by itself
idconcept.s7_desc: Minutes later the token expires and the platform issues a new one automatically. Nobody rotates anything by hand.
idconcept.s8_desc: Someone finds an old token in a log and tries to use it. It has expired, and the signature, issuer and audience no longer match, so IDIRA refuses it.
idconcept.s9_desc: A machine identity is issued by the platform, verified on every request and short-lived. There is no password in the code to leak, which is what the next concepts build on.

swaarch.title: Secure Workload Access architecture
swaarch.subtitle: How IDIRA Secure Workload Access (SWA) issues SPIFFE identities to your workloads: a control plane in Secrets Manager SaaS, an SWA Server and SWA Agents in your own infrastructure.

intro.issue_desc: Workloads receive SVIDs (X.509 and JWT) after attestation. The SWA Agent renews them before they expire, with no restart.
intro.federate_desc: A JWT-SVID is exchanged for temporary AWS, Azure or Google Cloud credentials through OIDC federation.
intro.exchange_desc: Workloads that still need a password authenticate to Secrets Manager with their JWT-SVID and fetch only what policy grants.

swaarch.flow_intro: Kubernetes and VM deployments use the SWA Server and SWA Agents. The control plane, inventory, audit and public JWKS live in Secrets Manager SaaS. Ports are shown on each connection.

flow.diagram_label: IDIRA Secure Workload Access architecture
flow.s1_title: 1. Two halves: control plane and data plane
flow.s1_desc: SWA is a SPIFFE implementation delivered as a feature of Secrets Manager. Secrets Manager SaaS is the control plane; the SWA Server and SWA Agents run in your infrastructure and issue the identities.
flow.s2_desc: In Secrets Manager you define the trust domain, the server group and the node groups. The SWA Server, registered with an authn_id and installed with Helm, connects to the tenant over HTTPS to retrieve its configuration.
flow.s3_desc: Secrets Manager publishes the trust domain OIDC discovery document and JWKS under /.well-known. Anyone who must verify a JWT-SVID, such as a cloud provider, reads the public keys there.
flow.s4_desc: The SWA Agent runs as a DaemonSet and presents a projected service account token (k8s_psat) on TCP 8443. The SWA Server validates it against the Kubernetes API and reads the swa_nodegroup label to place the node in a node group.
flow.s5_title: 5. VMs and other clusters through a load balancer
flow.s5_desc: Agents outside the server cluster reach it through a LoadBalancer Service that forwards TCP 8443. They attest with an X.509 machine certificate (x509pop) or the AWS Instance Identity Document.
flow.s6_desc: The workload calls the Workload API on a local Unix domain socket, with no network call and no credential. The agent checks its runtime attributes (namespace, service account, labels; or uid, path and binary hash on Unix).
flow.s7_desc: The agent obtains the SVID from the server and hands the workload an X.509-SVID, a JWT-SVID and the trust bundle. SWA records the workload under data/swa/trust-domains/<trust-domain>/workloads/, with no secret access by default.
flow.s8_desc: The SPIFFE ID sits in the X.509-SVID SAN URI, so two workloads authenticate each other over mTLS without shared API keys or hand-made certificates.
flow.s9_title: 9. Cloud access with no stored keys
flow.s9_desc: payments-api requests a JWT-SVID with the cloud audience (for AWS, sts.amazonaws.com). The cloud validates it against the public JWKS of the SWA issuer and returns temporary credentials, for example through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.
flow.s10_title: 10. Secret exchange when a credential is still needed
flow.s10_desc: For targets that are not SPIFFE-aware, orders-api presents its RSA-signed JWT-SVID to the Secrets Manager JWT authenticator, which maps the SPIFFE ID to the workload host and returns only the secrets that policy grants.
flow.s11_desc: SVIDs are short-lived and the SWA Agent renews them before they expire, with no restart. Secrets Manager keeps the workload inventory and the audit log.

swaarch.col_where: Where it runs and how it connects

sm.name: Secrets Manager SaaS (control plane)
sm.role: Defines trust domains, server groups, node groups and attestation policies. Provides the workload inventory, audit logging and the public JWKS endpoints.
sm.where: IDIRA cloud. SWA is available in US-EAST-1. Managed through the UI, REST API or the Terraform provider.

oidc.name: OIDC discovery and JWKS
oidc.role: Public issuer endpoints of each trust domain, used by relying parties and cloud providers to verify JWT-SVIDs.

server.name: SWA Server
server.role: Performs client (node) attestation, issues SVIDs and manages the trust domain signing keys. Retrieves configuration from and reports inventory to Secrets Manager.
server.where: Your Kubernetes cluster (Helm chart, namespace swa-system). Listens on 8443 for agents; replicaCount defaults to 1.

lb.name: Load balancer
lb.role: Exposes the SWA Server API to agents outside its cluster (VMs or another cluster). In-cluster agents use the Service DNS name instead.
lb.where: Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer forwarding TCP 8443; can be internal with cloud annotations.

agent.name: SWA Agent (Kubernetes)
agent.role: Exposes the Workload API, performs workload attestation and requests SVIDs from the server on behalf of local workloads.
agent.where: DaemonSet on every node; node attestation with k8s_psat (or k8s_jwt when the server cannot reach the API server).

vm.name: SWA Agent (VM)
vm.role: Same role on Unix or Linux machines, attesting processes with the unix workload attestor.
vm.where: System service installed with Ansible; node attestation with x509pop or AWS IID; connects to the server load balancer on 8443.

attestors.name: Node attestation
attestors.role: Verifies the connecting node before any workload on it gets an SVID: k8s_psat, k8s_jwt, x509pop or AWS IID (EC2).
attestors.where: Evaluated by the SWA Server against the server group policies; the node lands in a node group.

wapi.name: Workload API
wapi.role: Local API that workloads call to get their SVIDs and trust bundle, without network calls or pre-shared credentials.
wapi.where: Unix domain socket exposed by the agent (default /tmp/swa-agent/public/api.sock in Kubernetes).

svid.name: X.509-SVID and JWT-SVID
svid.role: Signed identity documents that prove the SPIFFE ID: X.509 for mTLS, JWT for federation and Secrets Manager authentication.
svid.where: Held by the workload; short-lived and renewed automatically by the agent.

cloud.name: Cloud federation
cloud.role: AWS IAM OIDC provider (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity), Azure federated identity credential, Google Workload Identity Federation: exchange a JWT-SVID for temporary credentials.
cloud.where: In each cloud account, trusting the public SWA issuer URL and the workload SPIFFE ID.

authn.name: Secrets Manager JWT authenticator
authn.role: Lets a workload trade its JWT-SVID for the secrets that policy grants (secret exchange).
authn.where: Secrets Manager SaaS; accepts RSA-signed JWTs only (RS* with RSA_*).

swaarch.ports_sub: Only values that the documentation gives. Where no port is documented, the protocol is shown.

p8443.path: Every SWA Agent to the SWA Server (or its load balancer)
p8443.purpose: SWA Server API: attestation and SVID requests. Must be reachable from every agent node.

pcp.path: SWA Server and agents to the tenant
pcp.purpose: Control plane configuration and the bootstrap trust bundle (.well-known/ca-bundles).

puds.path: Workload to the local SWA Agent

poidc.path: Cloud providers and verifiers to the tenant
poidc.purpose: OIDC discovery and JWKS; the issuer URL must be public and unauthenticated.

pk8s.path: SWA Server to the cluster API server
pk8s.purpose: Validates projected service account tokens for k8s_psat.

paws.purpose: ec2:DescribeInstances to verify instances attesting with AWS IID.

limits.i1: SWA is available in the US-EAST-1 region only.
limits.i2: The Secrets Manager JWT authenticator accepts RSA-signed JWTs only (RS* with RSA_*). Keep RSA signing on the trust domain for secret exchange; new trust domains default to RS512 with RSA_4096.
limits.i3: TCP 8443 on the SWA Server must be reachable from every node or VM that runs an agent; otherwise the agent fails at bootstrap and never attests.
limits.i4: For AWS and Google Cloud federation the issuer URL must be a public, unauthenticated HTTPS URL.
limits.i5: k8s_psat needs network access from the SWA Server to the Kubernetes API server; use k8s_jwt when that is not possible (for example hub and spoke).
limits.i6: New workload identities have no secret access by default: grant permissions before the workload needs secrets.
limits.i7: Migrating from another authenticator: SWA does not reuse the existing identity. Delete it, grant the new SPIFFE identity and plan a short interruption.
limits.i8: Without bootstrap.bundleSourceUrl, a server CA rotation requires a manual agent restart.
limits.i9: The agentless flow (swa_identity_sdk) applies to managed GCP compute such as Gemini Enterprise; it has no node groups and no Workload API socket.

practices.i1: Set bootstrap.bundleSourceUrl in production so agents recover automatically when the server CA rotates.
practices.i2: Expose the SWA Server through an internal load balancer when agents run outside its cluster, and open TCP 8443 early with the firewall team.
practices.i3: Restrict cloud roles to the expected SPIFFE ID (the JWT sub claim) and request the audience each provider expects.
practices.i4: Grant the SWA Server role only ec2:DescribeInstances when you use AWS IID attestation.
practices.i5: Use separate trust domains for separate administrative boundaries, such as production and non-production.
practices.i6: Prefer SPIFFE-aware access (mTLS, federation) and keep secret exchange for targets that still need a credential.
practices.i7: Manage trust domains, server groups and node groups as code with the REST API or the Terraform provider.
