ai_mcp.title: Secrets Manager MCP server
ai_mcp.subtitle: Lets an AI coding tool (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code Copilot) read and update IDIRA Secrets Manager through the Model Context Protocol: create branches, secrets and workloads, grant access, and generate the code that fetches the secret. The tested use case is migrating hard-coded secrets out of a repository.
ai_mcp.flow_title: From a hard-coded secret to an SDK call
ai_mcp.flow_lead: The AI tool starts the MCP server as a local container, the developer signs in as a dedicated user, and every tool call runs with that user's permissions on its own branch.
ai_mcp.how_lead: Everything runs on the developer machine except Identity and Secrets Manager. There is no service account with standing access: the MCP server only acts after an interactive sign-in.
roles: AI tool (MCP client)
Claude Code, Cursor or VS Code Copilot. Starts the container through its MCP configuration (.mcp.json or .vscode/mcp.json) and talks to it over stdio.
MCP server container
Image downloaded from the Marketplace and loaded with docker load. Runs with -i (stdio) and -p 8080:8080 for the OAuth2 callback.
Idira Identity OAuth2 client
Custom OAuth2 client with redirect http://localhost:8080/callback. Its authorize endpoint signs the developer in; a confidential service account is the client_id.
Dedicated Secrets Manager user
User in the Secrets Manager User role, member of a group that owns only the mcp-server branch (create, read, update). Every action is audited under this user.
IDIRA Secrets Manager
Receives the REST calls: branches, secrets (variables), workloads (hosts) and permissions, always inside data/.
ai_mcp.tools_lead: Commands you can type in the AI tool, or that the model calls on its own while following a prompt.
tools: Returns the Identity sign-in URL. Run it first.
Completes the sign-in after the browser login (you can also type done).
Creates a branch, which must start with data/.
Creates a secret (variable) and offers to grant workload access to it.
Creates a workload (host) and returns its API key.
Grants a workload read or execute on a secret.
Lists what the authenticated user can see.
Generates code that fetches the secret: Ruby, Go, Java or curl.
ai_mcp.setup_lead: Requirements: Docker on the host, an Identity OAuth2 client with a service account, and a dedicated Secrets Manager user.
setup: Create a dedicated user in Identity Administration and add it to the Secrets Manager User role.
Load a policy that creates the mcp-users group, adds the user, and makes the group owner of the mcp-server branch with create, read and update.

Create a service account (Is OAuth confidential client) and a custom OAuth2 client with redirect http://localhost:8080/callback; give both the service account and the dedicated user permission on the client.
Download the MCP server package from the Marketplace and load it with docker load -i.
Configure the AI tool to run the container with the environment variables below (.mcp.json for Claude Code, .vscode/mcp.json for Copilot).
In the AI tool, run get_auth_url, sign in with the dedicated user, then run authenticate.
ai_mcp.env_lead: All required except the log level. The container needs -i (stdio) and -p 8080:8080.
env: Tenant API endpoint, for example acme.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud.
Application ID of the Identity OAuth2 client.
Login name of the client's service account.
Issuer URL shown on the OAuth2 client, for example https://acme.id.cyberark.cloud.
when: Use a dedicated, least-privileged user restricted to one branch, never an admin: the agent acts with the user's full authority.
Review the generated changes: the tested flow scans the code, creates branch, secrets and workload, replaces the literals with SDK calls and writes a .env added to .gitignore.
If the generated code has placeholders, call create_workload and then generate_fetch_code.
Keep port 8080 free for the OAuth2 callback; if sign-in fails, clear browser cookies and run get_auth_url again.
Since the December 2025 release the Create Workload page also offers AI Agent and MCP Server workload types.
diff: SaaS only: the MCP server is documented for Secrets Manager SaaS and uses Idira Identity OAuth2 for sign-in.
Self-Hosted has no equivalent MCP server in the documentation.
Released as beta on March 4, 2026; the package version listed in the docs is 0.1.0-beta.
limits: Development environments only: not supported in production.
The MCP server does not enforce a boundary between the AI agent and the authenticated user: the agent can reach every secret that user can reach.
You are responsible for every action the agent performs and for securing the MCP server against unauthorized access.
Tested with Claude Code v2.075 and the claude-sonnet-4-5 model; other clients are compatible but not listed as tested.
create_workload returns a workload API key: the generated .env holds a credential, so keep it out of version control.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: an AI tool starts the Secrets Manager MCP server, the developer signs in through Identity, and the AI creates a branch, secrets and a workload, then replaces a hard-coded secret with an SDK call.
flow.s1_desc: The repository has a secret written in the source code. The goal is to move it to Secrets Manager without giving the AI an admin credential.
flow.s2_desc: An administrator creates a dedicated user and a policy: the mcp-users group owns only the mcp-server branch, with create, read and update. An OAuth2 client in Identity will sign this user in.
flow.s3_title: The AI tool starts the server
flow.s3_desc: From .mcp.json, the AI tool runs the container with docker run -i -p 8080:8080 and talks to it over stdio. The first tool to call is get_auth_url.
flow.s4_desc: The browser opens the Identity login. The developer signs in as the dedicated user and Identity redirects to localhost:8080/callback, giving the MCP server an OAuth2 session.
flow.s5_desc: Back in the AI tool, authenticate (or done) connects the MCP server to Secrets Manager as that user. whoami confirms who the agent is acting as.
flow.s6_desc: The developer asks: scan the repository for hard-coded secrets, upload them and replace them. The model calls create_branch, for example data/mcp-server/my-app.
flow.s7_desc: For each hard-coded value the model calls create_secret. The value now lives in Secrets Manager, inside the branch the user owns.
flow.s8_desc: create_workload creates a workload (host) for the application and returns its API key; grant_secret_permission lets it read the new secrets.
flow.s9_desc: generate_fetch_code returns SDK code (Ruby, Go, Java or curl). The model replaces the literal, writes the workload credentials to a .env and adds it to .gitignore.

ai_swa.badge: AI agents · SPIFFE · Secure Workload Access
ai_swa.title: SPIFFE identities for AI agents
ai_swa.subtitle: An AI agent does not need an API key in a file or environment variable. It proves what it is through attestation, receives a short-lived JWT-SVID and uses it with each service: IDIRA Secrets Manager for secrets, and model providers such as the Claude API or Google Cloud for inference.
ai_swa.flow_lead: The same agent asks for one JWT-SVID per audience. Secrets Manager and the Claude API each verify the signature against the trust domain's public keys and map the SPIFFE ID to their own permissions.
ai_swa.how_lead: The agent never holds a long-lived credential: tokens are minted on demand, scoped by audience, and expire in minutes.
roles: SWA Agent (or SPIRE agent)
Attests the agent process and serves the SPIFFE Workload API on a local socket: /tmp/swa-agent/public/api.sock in Kubernetes, /run/swa-agent/api.sock on VMs.
Trust domain OIDC issuer
Public, unauthenticated /.well-known/openid-configuration and JWKS endpoint, published by Secrets Manager for each SWA trust domain. Relying parties fetch signing keys from it.
AI agent workload
Your agent code. Fetches JWT-SVIDs through spiffe-helper (token file) or a Workload API client (py-spiffe, go-spiffe) and keeps them in memory.
Secrets Manager authn-jwt
JWT authenticator with jwks-uri, issuer, token-app-property=sub and identity-path=data/spiffe-apps. The workload is named after the SPIFFE ID and created with the AI Agent type.
Claude API federation
Federation issuer (fdis_), rule (fdrl_) matching sub and aud, target service account (svac_), workspace and OAuth scope. Returns an access token that the SDK refreshes.
ai_swa.variants_lead: Same idea, different relying party. Choose by where the agent runs and what it needs to reach.

variants.title: Secrets Manager (authn-jwt)
variants.how: JWT authenticator pointing at the SPIFFE OIDC discovery JWKS. The sub claim maps to a workload in data/spiffe-apps that belongs to the authenticator's apps group and to the Safe consumers group.

variants.title: Claude API
variants.who: Agent calls Claude without an API key
variants.how: Register the trust domain as a Custom OIDC issuer in the Claude Console, create a rule pinned to the full SPIFFE ID and to the audience, and set the federation variables. The SDK does the token exchange.

variants.title: Gemini Enterprise
variants.how: SWA server group with gcp_service_account attestation (allowed project IDs). The agent sends its Google ID token to the SWA server through the SWA Python SDK and receives a JWT-SVID, usable with Google Workload Identity Federation.

when: Pin each rule to one workload: use the full SPIFFE ID, not a trailing *, which would let every workload under that prefix act as the target.
Always set an audience matcher, and create one rule and service account per scope instead of widening one.
Use the narrowest scope: workspace:inference for an agent that only sends inference requests.
With spiffe-helper, keep the token file in a memory-backed emptyDir readable only by the agent; with the Workload API client the token never touches disk.
Unset ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_PROFILE: they take precedence over federation, even as empty strings.
Gemini Enterprise: one dedicated Google Cloud service account per agent, never shared.
diff: SaaS: Secure Workload Access is part of Secrets Manager SaaS, which publishes the trust domain's OIDC issuer and JWKS; there is no discovery component to deploy.
SaaS: the AI Agent and MCP Server workload types appear on the Create Workload page.
Self-Hosted: these AI agent guides are not in the Self-Hosted documentation. Generic JWT authentication against your own SPIRE OIDC discovery provider follows the regular authn-jwt pages.
limits: Secure Workload Access is available only in the US-EAST-1 region.
Claude API federation accepts JWT-SVIDs only; X.509 SVIDs cannot be exchanged for an Anthropic access token.
The issuer URL registered with Anthropic must match the iss claim character by character, including the scheme and any trailing slash.
The Anthropic access token lives for the lesser of token_lifetime_seconds and twice the JWT-SVID's remaining lifetime; with the default 300-second SVID, the SVID usually governs.
Gemini Enterprise: a standard Kubernetes Ingress does not carry the SWA gRPC API (port 8443) without TCP passthrough; expose the SWA server with a LoadBalancer service.
Protect the Workload API socket and any token file: any process that can read them can obtain the agent's access.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: the SWA Agent attests an AI agent and issues JWT-SVIDs; the agent authenticates to Secrets Manager with one and fetches a secret, then exchanges another for a Claude API access token. Both services verify signatures with the trust domain's public JWKS.
flow.s1_desc: The AI agent has no API key in code, files or environment variables. It needs a secret from Secrets Manager and access to a model.
flow.s2_desc: The agent calls the SPIFFE Workload API on the local socket. The SWA Agent attests the process (node group policy in Kubernetes, VM or cloud identity) and assigns its SPIFFE ID.
flow.s3_desc: The agent asks for a JWT-SVID with audience conjur. It is short-lived and its sub claim is the SPIFFE ID.
flow.s4_desc: The agent sends the JWT-SVID to authn-jwt/spiffe-auth. Secrets Manager fetches the trust domain's public JWKS and checks signature and issuer.
flow.s5_desc: token-app-property=sub and identity-path=data/spiffe-apps map the SPIFFE ID to a workload of type AI Agent, a member of the authenticator's apps group.
flow.s6_desc: Secrets Manager returns a short-lived access token. With it the agent reads the secret through the REST API; policy allows it because the workload is in the Safe consumers group.
flow.s7_desc: For the model provider the agent asks for a new JWT-SVID with audience https://api.anthropic.com. One audience per relying party keeps tokens from being replayed elsewhere.
flow.s8_desc: The SDK posts the JWT-SVID to /v1/oauth/token (jwt-bearer). Anthropic verifies it with the registered issuer's JWKS and matches the federation rule on sub and aud.
flow.s9_desc: Anthropic returns an access token for the mapped service account and workspace, for example 600 seconds. The SDK refreshes it before it expires.
flow.s10_desc: The agent calls messages.create with the narrow workspace:inference scope. The call is attributed to the service account, and no API key ever existed.

sm_dynamic.flow_title: How it works today, step by step
sm_dynamic.title: Dynamic secrets
sm_dynamic.subtitle: Instead of storing a long-lived cloud key, IDIRA Secrets Manager creates a fresh credential at the moment the workload asks for it. The credential is valid for a short TTL and then stops working on its own: there is nothing to rotate and little left to leak.
sm_dynamic.flow_lead: Example with AWS: the workload reads a variable under data/dynamic and receives temporary STS credentials that expire after the TTL.
sm_dynamic.how_lead: An issuer holds how to reach the cloud; a dynamic secret says what to create; policy says who may get it.
roles: Issuer
Created by a Secrets Manager admin. Holds the target type (aws or gcp), the maximum TTL (900 to 43,200 seconds) and references to the cloud credentials stored as secrets, never the raw values.
Cloud credentials of the issuer

AWS: an IAM user access key ID and secret access key with sts:GetFederationToken or sts:AssumeRole. GCP: a service account key that can create access tokens. Stored as secrets, ideally synced from PAM.
consumers group
conjur/issuers/{issuer}/delegation/consumers. Its members may create dynamic secrets that use the issuer.
Dynamic secret (variable)
A variable under data/dynamic with annotations dynamic/issuer and dynamic/method (federation-token, assume-role or access-token), plus optional TTL, region, inline policy or role ARN.
Workload (host)
Needs read and execute on the variable. A normal GET of the secret triggers the creation of the credential.
Cloud provider
AWS STS returns access key, secret key and session token; GCP returns a short-lived service account access token. Both expire after the TTL.
when: Workloads that call AWS or GCP APIs and today use a static access key or service account key.
Jobs and pipelines that need cloud access for minutes, not months.
Least privilege per workload: an inline policy (AWS) or scope list (GCP) narrows each credential.
Reducing the blast radius of a leak: a stolen credential expires by itself within the TTL.
diff: SaaS: AWS (federation token or assumed role) and GCP (service account access token).
Self-Hosted: AWS dynamic secrets (federation token or assumed role) are documented; GCP is documented for SaaS only.
Both: issuer created via UI, REST API (POST /api/issuers/conjur) or CLI (conjur issuer create); the secret lives under data/dynamic.
Self-Hosted: the role that creates the issuer needs read permission on the two credential variables, and new issuers must use secret references (inline key values are rejected).
limits: Only cloud targets are covered: AWS on both platforms, GCP on SaaS. Databases and other targets are not dynamic secrets here; use rotation instead.
TTL is bounded: minimum 900 seconds (15 minutes), maximum 43,200 seconds (12 hours), and never above the issuer maximum. Without a TTL the issuer maximum applies.
The issuer depends on a long-lived IAM user key or GCP service account key. Keep it in PAM with rotation and give it only sts:AssumeRole or sts:GetFederationToken (or the token creator role).
Dynamic secrets must be created under data/dynamic, and you must own the branch (be in the group that owns it) to see or manage them.
To use an issuer you must be in its consumers group; only a Secrets Manager admin creates issuers.
Each read creates a new credential. Cache it for its TTL in the application instead of reading it on every call.

flow.diagram_label: AWS dynamic secret issued by IDIRA Secrets Manager
flow.s1_desc: The workload needs AWS access. No AWS key is stored with it: Secrets Manager will create one on demand.
flow.s2_title: 2. The issuer points to the IAM user keys
flow.s2_desc: The admin created my-aws-issuer. It references the IAM user access key ID and secret access key stored as secrets (synced from PAM), and sets the maximum TTL.
flow.s3_desc: With any authenticator (JWT, AWS IAM, API key...) the workload proves its identity and receives a short-lived access token.
flow.s4_desc: A normal GET on data/dynamic/my-aws-dynamic-secret. Policy checks that the host has read and execute on the variable.
flow.s5_desc: Using the issuer keys, Secrets Manager calls AssumeRole (or GetFederationToken) with the TTL and the optional inline policy. STS creates temporary credentials.
flow.s6_desc: The response carries access_key_id, secret_access_key, session_token and the TTL (1200 seconds here). Nothing long-lived reached the workload.
flow.s7_desc: The workload signs its AWS API calls with the temporary credentials, limited by the role and the inline policy.
flow.s8_desc: After 1200 seconds AWS rejects the credentials. Nothing needs to be revoked; the workload simply reads the dynamic secret again for a new set.

sm_certs.flow_title: How it works today, step by step
sm_certs.title: Certificates for workloads
sm_certs.subtitle: A workload can ask IDIRA Secrets Manager for an X.509 certificate the same way it asks for a secret. Secrets Manager forwards the request to Palo Alto Networks Certificate Manager, SaaS, and the certificate comes back signed by the CA behind the chosen issuing template.
sm_certs.flow_lead: Issue request: Secrets Manager generates the CSR, Certificate Manager signs it, and the workload receives certificate, chain and private key in one response.
sm_certs.how_lead: Three products meet here: Identity authenticates Secrets Manager to Certificate Manager, Certificate Manager applies the template, Secrets Manager applies policy.
roles: Certificate Manager issuer
Issuer of type pki_cert_mgr_saas created by a member of Conjur_Cloud_Admins. Holds the service account token URL, the default zone and the allowed zones.
Identity service user

An OAuth confidential client in Idira Identity. Its credentials are stored in Secrets Manager (synced from PAM with the Identity Service User CPM plugin, or as static secrets) and used to get a token for Certificate Manager.
Certificate Manager service account
Custom API Integration account with the Certificate Issuance scope, trusting the Identity tenant OIDC issuer and the service user UUID.
Zone
application\issuing-template in Certificate Manager. The template decides CA, key algorithms and maximum validity. A request may pick any allowed zone; otherwise the default zone is used.
operators and executors groups
Created with the issuer. Operators (conjur/issuers/{issuer}/operators) add workloads to executors; executors (.../delegation/executors) may request certificates.
Workload
Authenticates as usual, then calls POST /api/issuers/{issuer}/issue (Secrets Manager builds the CSR) or /sign (the workload sends its own CSR).
when: Workloads that need TLS or mTLS server or client certificates without opening tickets or handling CSRs by hand.
Teams that already authenticate to Secrets Manager and want one API for secrets and certificates.
Keeping the corporate CA and templates (validity, key type) under Certificate Manager control while developers self-serve.
Sign requests when the private key must never leave the workload: only the CSR travels.
diff: SaaS: available through the Certificate Manager issuer (Certificate Manager, SaaS).
Self-Hosted: no Certificate Manager issuer is documented for Secrets Manager Self-Hosted.
For SPIFFE workload identity certificates (X.509-SVID) see Secure Workload Access instead; this page is about certificates from your CA.
limits: SaaS only, and only with Palo Alto Networks Certificate Manager, SaaS as the back end.
Setup spans three admins: Identity (service user), Certificate Manager (application, issuing template, service account) and Secrets Manager (issuer and groups).
The Identity tenant ID in the issuer and JWKS URLs must be lowercase.
ttl must be an ISO 8601 duration (for example P3M). Without it the template validity is used; key_type must be one the template allows (RSA takes precedence over EC when omitted).
Issue requests store certificate and private key in Secrets Manager; sign requests store only the certificate. Keys and CSRs are not listed as resources in UI, API or CLI.
To replace a certificate with the same common_name, SANs and zone (for example to change validity) the request must set the replace option.
The workload must belong to the issuer executors group (execute permission); otherwise the request returns 403.
docs: Palo Alto Networks Certificate Manager issuer

flow.diagram_label: Certificate issued to a workload through IDIRA Secrets Manager and Certificate Manager
flow.s1_desc: The workload will serve TLS. Instead of a ticket to the PKI team, it asks Secrets Manager, which brokers the request to Certificate Manager.
flow.s2_title: 2. The issuer can reach Certificate Manager
flow.s2_desc: The issuer uses the Identity service user credentials stored in Secrets Manager to get a token for the Certificate Manager service account.
flow.s3_desc: With its usual authenticator (JWT, AWS IAM, certificate...) the workload receives a short-lived access token.
flow.s4_desc: POST /api/issuers/{issuer}/issue with common_name, optional SANs, ttl (P3M) and zone. Secrets Manager checks that the workload is in the executors group.
flow.s5_desc: For an issue request Secrets Manager generates the key pair and CSR, then forwards them with the zone to Certificate Manager.
flow.s6_desc: The issuing template of the zone decides CA, key type and validity. The signed certificate and its chain return to Secrets Manager.
flow.s7_desc: One JSON with certificate, chain and private_key (private_key is empty for sign requests, where the workload sent its own CSR).
flow.s8_desc: The workload presents the certificate; clients that trust the corporate CA complete the handshake.

sm_rotation.flow_title: How it works today, step by step
sm_rotation.title: Secret rotation
sm_rotation.subtitle: The longer a secret stays the same, the more it is worth to an attacker. In IDIRA Secrets Manager the recommended path is to let the PAM Central Policy Manager (CPM) rotate the password on the target and sync the new value to Secrets Manager, where workloads read it.
sm_rotation.flow_lead: The CPM changes the database password, the Vault keeps the new value and the sync delivers it to Secrets Manager. The workload that re-reads the secret keeps working.
sm_rotation.how_lead: Rotation happens in PAM; Secrets Manager distributes the current value to workloads.
roles: CPM (Central Policy Manager)
Part of Privilege Cloud and PAM Self-Hosted. Changes the password on the target system according to the platform policy (for example every 30 days) and verifies it.
Safe and account
The account lives in a Safe that is associated with Secrets Manager. Each account becomes secrets under data/vault/{safe}/{account}: one for the password and one per property.
Sync (ConjurSync / Conjur Sync user)
Member of the Safe with Use, Retrieve and List accounts. Privilege Cloud changes sync in near real time; PAM Self-Hosted syncs every minute.
Workload
Reads the secret through Secrets Manager. It must fetch the value again when a login fails or on a schedule, instead of caching it forever.
Dual accounts
Two accounts that take turns: one is in use while the other rotates, so a workload never reads a password just before it changes.
Local rotators (Self-Hosted)
Built-in rotation through rotation/rotator and rotation/ttl annotations, for AWS secret access keys and PostgreSQL passwords. For a single server or development only.
when: Database, service account and cloud passwords that applications use and must change regularly.
Credentials already onboarded in PAM that now also need to reach applications.
Compliance requirements for periodic password change without application downtime (with dual accounts).
When the target cannot issue short-lived credentials; for AWS and GCP prefer dynamic secrets.
diff: SaaS: rotation comes from Privilege Cloud or PAM Self-Hosted through Safe sync. Static secrets created in Secrets Manager are never rotated automatically.
Self-Hosted: the same PAM CPM path is the recommended one for clusters (Vault Synchronizer).
Self-Hosted only: local rotators (AWS secret access key, PostgreSQL password) for a single Secrets Manager server or a development environment.
Both: dual accounts are supported for secrets synced from PAM.
limits: Secrets Manager SaaS has no built-in rotator: a secret only rotates if it comes from PAM. A static secret must be updated by hand.
Self-Hosted local rotation is disabled by default, is meant for a single server or development, and must be enabled again after every Leader upgrade and after any failover.
Local rotators exist only for AWS secret access keys and PostgreSQL passwords; each requires variables with fixed names (for example region, access_key_id, secret_access_key).
A local rotation that fails is retried after 2/5 of the TTL (with a TTL of 30 days, every 12 days) until it succeeds.
After the first value is set, a local rotation runs almost immediately (within 1 second); after that it follows rotation/ttl in ISO 8601 (for example P1D).
Applications that cache the old password fail after a rotation. Read the secret again on authentication errors or use dual accounts.
docs: Sync Safes and accounts from PAM (SaaS)

flow.diagram_label: Password rotated by the PAM CPM and delivered through IDIRA Secrets Manager
flow.l_sync: sync · near real time to 1 min
flow.s1_desc: The database password is v1 in the target, in the PAM Vault, in Secrets Manager and in the running application.
flow.s2_desc: The platform policy says it is time. The CPM sets a new random password v2 on the database and stores it in the Vault account.
flow.s3_desc: The Safe is associated with Secrets Manager. The new value replaces the secret under data/vault/{safe}/{account}: near real time from Privilege Cloud, within a minute from PAM Self-Hosted.
flow.s4_desc: The application still holds v1 in memory. Its next login fails: this is why caching a secret forever breaks rotation.
flow.s5_title: 5. The workload reads the secret again
flow.s5_desc: On the authentication error the application authenticates to Secrets Manager and fetches the secret again, receiving v2.
flow.s6_desc: Login with v2 succeeds. With dual accounts this gap disappears: the application uses one account while the other one rotates.

k8s_spmodes.title: Secrets Provider: deployment modes
k8s_spmodes.subtitle: The Secrets Provider for Kubernetes pulls secrets from Secrets Manager and hands them to the application in one of two ways: inside a native Kubernetes Secret or as a file on a shared volume (Push-to-File). It can run as an init container, a sidecar, a Kubernetes Job or a standalone Deployment.
k8s_spmodes.flow_lead: Pick the destination to see the flow. The diagram shows the Provider inside the application Pod (init container or sidecar), the most common setup.
k8s_spmodes.mode_note_k8s: The Provider reads the conjur-map of each Kubernetes Secret listed for the Pod, fetches the matching variables and writes the values into those Secrets through the Kubernetes API. The application consumes them as usual: environment variables or a mounted volume.
k8s_spmodes.mode_note_p2f: The Provider reads secret groups from Pod annotations (Downward API volume), fetches the variables and renders one file per group on a volume shared with the application container. No Kubernetes Secret is created.

flow.k8s_diagram_label: Diagram: the Secrets Provider authenticates to Secrets Manager, fetches the mapped variables and writes them into a Kubernetes Secret that the application consumes.
flow.k8s_s1_desc: The Provider starts in the application Pod and, with the Pod's service account (RBAC get on Secrets), reads each Kubernetes Secret listed in K8S_SECRETS. Its conjur-map says which Secrets Manager variable fills which key.
flow.k8s_s2_desc: The Provider authenticates to Secrets Manager with the configured authenticator, usually authn-jwt with the projected service account token (SaaS and Self-Hosted; Self-Hosted also offers authn-k8s). The host policy is checked and an access token comes back.
flow.k8s_s3_desc: With the access token, the Provider retrieves only the variables the host may read, or every allowed variable when fetch all is used.
flow.k8s_s4_desc: For each mapping, the Provider writes the value into the Kubernetes Secret through the API server (RBAC update or patch). Nothing is stored in the image or in the manifest.
flow.k8s_s5_desc: The application container starts and reads the Secret like any native Kubernetes Secret: envFrom, secretKeyRef or a mounted volume. As an init container, the Provider has already exited.
flow.k8s_s6_desc: Only as a sidecar: at each interval (conjur.org/secrets-refresh-interval) the Provider fetches again and compares SHA-256 checksums. A rotated value is written to the Secret; a deleted or revoked variable is removed from it.
flow.k8s_s7_desc: Mounted Secret volumes pick up the new value on their own; environment variables only after a restart. To restart automatically, combine with Reloader.
flow.p2f_diagram_label: Diagram: the Secrets Provider reads secret groups from Pod annotations, fetches the variables from Secrets Manager and writes secrets files to a volume shared with the application.
flow.p2f_s1_desc: The Provider starts in the Pod and parses the Pod annotations exposed through a Downward API volume. Each secret group (conjur.org/secret-group.*) lists the variable paths, the file format and how values map to fields.
flow.p2f_s2_desc: The Provider authenticates to Secrets Manager with the configured authenticator, usually authn-jwt with the projected service account token (SaaS and Self-Hosted; Self-Hosted also offers authn-k8s). The host policy is checked and an access token comes back.
flow.p2f_s3_desc: The Provider reads every Secrets Manager variable needed across all secret groups.
flow.p2f_s4_desc: For each group, the Provider renders a file (YAML by default, or JSON, dotenv, bash, properties or a custom template) and writes it to the shared volume, with permissions 644 by default.
flow.p2f_s5_desc: The application container starts and reads the file from the shared volume, the way it already reads configuration files. No Kubernetes Secret object exists.
flow.p2f_s6_desc: Only as a sidecar: at each interval the Provider fetches again and compares SHA-256 checksums. A rotated value rewrites the file (also if the app deleted it after reading); a deleted or revoked variable removes the file.
flow.p2f_s7_desc: The application must re-read the file to use a rotated value. Push-to-File works with the init container and the sidecar only, not with the Job or standalone modes.

k8s_spmodes.deploy_lead: The same image, four ways to run it. Where it runs decides which destinations and which update behavior you get.
deploy: Inside the application Pod; runs to completion before the app starts
No: secrets are delivered once, at Pod start
Inside the application Pod, next to the app for its whole life
Yes: refresh interval, SHA-256 change detection, rotation
Its own Pod (application mode, Helm chart); serves every app in the namespace
No: runs once; rerun the Job (for example from a CronJob) to refresh
Long-running Deployment (Helm chart), outside the application Pods
Yes: reconciles labeled Secrets every 5 minutes by default and when they change, across allowlisted namespaces
k8s_spmodes.dest_lead: Both destinations use the same authentication and the same secrets; what changes is where the value lands and how the app reads it.
dest: A native Kubernetes Secret in the namespace, updated through the API server
A file on a volume shared inside the Pod; no Kubernetes Secret object
The K8S_SECRETS list plus a conjur-map in each Secret
Pod annotations per secret group (conjur.org/secret-group.*), read through the Downward API
envFrom, secretKeyRef or a mounted Secret volume
Opens the file: yaml, json, dotenv, bash, properties or a custom template
get plus update or patch on the mapped Secrets
Not needed for Secrets: values are written inside the Pod
Init container, sidecar, Job and standalone
Apps already built around Kubernetes Secrets
Apps that read config files, or teams that keep secrets out of Kubernetes Secret objects
k8s_spmodes.roles_lead: Who does what in a Secrets Provider deployment.
roles: Secrets Provider
Image cyberark-secrets-provider-for-k8s: authenticates, fetches and delivers the secrets. Runs as init container, sidecar, Job or standalone Deployment.
Secrets Manager host
The Provider's workload identity in policy (for authn-jwt, named after the namespace and service account), with read access to the variables.
Authenticator
authn-jwt with the projected service account token, authn-iam, authn-azure or authn-gcp. Self-Hosted also supports authn-k8s (mutual TLS).
Golden ConfigMap / conjur-connect
Secrets Manager connection details that the Provider reads as environment variables.
Kubernetes Secret + conjur-map
Kubernetes Secrets mode: the target object; conjur-map maps each key to a variable path.
Pod annotations (Downward API)
Push-to-File mode: secret groups with variable paths, file format, file path and permissions.
Shared volume
Push-to-File mode: a volume mounted by both containers, where the files are written.
Helm chart
Deploys the Job and standalone options with their RBAC. Standalone manages Secrets labeled conjur.org/managed-by-provider: "true".
caps: Fetch all
Map every variable the host can read instead of listing them. Keys become the variable path with / replaced by . (trim-path-segments shortens them).
File formats
yaml (default), json, dotenv, bash, properties or template (Go template from an annotation or a ConfigMap mounted at /conjur/templates).
Base64 decoding
content-type: base64 decodes values stored Base64-encoded in Secrets Manager.
Change detection
The sidecar compares SHA-256 checksums at each interval; standalone reconciles at its refresh interval and when a labeled Secret changes.
Revocation
If a variable is deleted or the host loses access, the Provider removes the value from the Secret or deletes the file.
Automatic restart
The Job and standalone options can enable Reloader (autoReload.enabled) to roll Deployments when a Secret changes.
when: Apps that already read Kubernetes Secrets and should not change code: Kubernetes Secrets mode.
Apps that read a config file, or when secrets should not exist as Kubernetes Secret objects: Push-to-File.
Secrets that rotate while the Pod runs: the sidecar (or standalone, for Kubernetes Secrets).
Many apps in one namespace that need the secrets once: the Job, deployed with the Helm chart.
One central provider keeping labeled Secrets in sync across several namespaces: standalone.
Short-lived Pods that only need secrets at startup: the init container is the lightest option.
diff: Availability
Every option (init container, sidecar, Job, standalone) and both destinations are documented for SaaS and Self-Hosted.
Authenticators
SaaS: authn-jwt, authn-iam, authn-azure, authn-gcp. Self-Hosted: the same, plus authn-k8s (certificate based, mutual TLS).
Endpoint
SaaS: the Secrets Manager SaaS tenant. Self-Hosted: the Leader or, more often, a Follower close to the cluster.
Configuration
Same annotations, conjur-map and Helm values; only the connection details change.
limits: Updates after start only with the sidecar (and standalone). An init container or a Job delivers secrets once; the Job must be rerun, for example by a CronJob.
Push-to-File works only with the init container and the sidecar. Standalone supports Kubernetes Secrets only and does not accept an explicit k8sSecrets list.
Job (application mode): up to 50 secrets with variable paths of about 100 characters on average. For more, deploy several Secrets Providers.

Fetch all: at most 500 secrets (error CSPFK010D), no aliases (keys are the full paths), and the bash, dotenv and properties formats are not supported. Paths that collapse into the same key fail (CSPFK098E).
Fetch all widens what a compromised host exposes: keep the host scoped to one app and a few variables (least privilege).
Containers that read secrets as environment variables only see a new value after a restart; mounted volumes update on their own. Reloader automates the restart.
Custom templates cannot reference a variable path directly (they are validated before the secrets are fetched): use aliases.
Standalone: a wider namespaceAllowlist means a wider RBAC surface (often a ClusterRole) and more load on the Secrets Manager and Kubernetes APIs.

k8s_reloader.title: Reloader: automatic restart
k8s_reloader.subtitle: When a Kubernetes Secret changes, Reloader rolls the Deployments and StatefulSets that use it, so new Pods start with the new value. It is an optional part of the Secrets Provider Helm chart (application and standalone modes).
k8s_reloader.flow_lead: Pick the Secrets Provider mode. Reloader behaves the same in both; what changes is who notices the new secret.
k8s_reloader.mode_note_standalone: Standalone: the Secrets Provider runs as a Deployment and refreshes on its own interval, so a new value travels from Secrets Manager to the Kubernetes Secret and on to the Pods with nothing else involved.
k8s_reloader.mode_note_job: Application mode: the Secrets Provider is a Job that runs once. To pick up a new value, an external trigger such as a CronJob must rerun the Job; Reloader takes it from there.

flow.standalone_diagram_label: Diagram: in standalone mode the Secrets Provider Deployment detects a changed secret on its refresh interval, updates the Kubernetes Secret, and Reloader rolls the annotated Deployment.
flow.standalone_s1_desc: A value changes in Secrets Manager: a manual update or a rotation.
flow.standalone_s2_desc: The standalone Secrets Provider runs all the time and, at its refresh interval (five minutes by default) or when a labeled Secret changes, starts a reconciliation.
flow.standalone_s3_desc: The Provider authenticates with its service account identity and fetches the current value from Secrets Manager.
flow.standalone_s4_desc: The Provider writes v2 into the Kubernetes Secret (labeled conjur.org/managed-by-provider: "true").
flow.standalone_s5_desc: Reloader watches the Kubernetes Secrets in its scope and detects that db-credentials changed.
flow.standalone_s6_desc: Reloader triggers a rolling restart of each Deployment or StatefulSet annotated with conjur.org/automatic-restart or conjur.org/restart-secrets that references this Secret.
flow.standalone_s7_desc: New Pods read v2 when they start, even apps that read secrets only from environment variables. Standalone plus Reloader keeps Pods current with no scheduled Job.
flow.job_diagram_label: Diagram: in application mode a CronJob reruns the Secrets Provider Job, the Job updates the Kubernetes Secret, and Reloader rolls the annotated Deployment.
flow.job_s1_desc: A value changes in Secrets Manager: a manual update or a rotation.
flow.job_s2_desc: The Job finished after its first run, so nothing is watching Secrets Manager. An external trigger, for example a CronJob, starts the Secrets Provider Job again on a schedule.
flow.job_s3_desc: The Provider authenticates with its service account identity and fetches the current value from Secrets Manager.
flow.job_s4_desc: The Job writes v2 into the Kubernetes Secrets mapped for the namespace and completes.
flow.job_s5_desc: Reloader watches the Kubernetes Secrets in its scope and detects that db-credentials changed.
flow.job_s6_desc: Reloader triggers a rolling restart of each Deployment or StatefulSet annotated with conjur.org/automatic-restart or conjur.org/restart-secrets that references this Secret.
flow.job_s7_desc: Freshness depends on the CronJob schedule. Reloader is a separate, always-on Deployment, even though the Provider itself is a short-lived Job.

k8s_reloader.roles_lead: Reloader is open source (Stakater, Apache License 2.0) and is installed as a subchart of the Secrets Provider Helm chart.
roles: Secrets Provider (Helm chart)
Writes Secrets Manager values into Kubernetes Secrets, in application mode (Job) or standalone mode (Deployment).
Reloader
Persistent Deployment that watches Kubernetes Secrets in its scope and triggers rolling restarts.
Annotated workload
Deployment or StatefulSet with conjur.org/automatic-restart or conjur.org/restart-secrets that references the Secret directly.
External trigger
Application mode only: a CronJob (or similar) that reruns the Secrets Provider Job on a schedule.
Reloader RBAC
Separate from the Provider's: list and watch Secrets; get, update and patch Deployments, DaemonSets and StatefulSets; Events; Leases when HA is on.
k8s_reloader.ann_lead: Annotate the Deployment or StatefulSet. The Pod spec must reference the Secret through envFrom, env.valueFrom.secretKeyRef or a volume.
ann: Restart when any Kubernetes Secret the workload references is updated.
Restart only when the named Secret changes. Accepts a comma-separated list, for example db-credentials,api-keys.
k8s_reloader.cfg_lead: Reloader stays off until you enable it in the Secrets Provider chart values.yaml.
cfg: Turns Reloader on (installs the subchart and its RBAC).
false by default: watches only the Helm release namespace. Must be true when standalone.namespaceAllowlist is * or lists several namespaces.
Several replicas with leader election (Lease objects), so one replica down does not miss updates.
Pinned to the bundled image. When you mirror the image or change the tag, update both.
modes: Nobody, until the Job is rerun
The Provider, at each refresh interval or Secret change
A CronJob or another trigger to rerun the Job
Reloader (always on); the Job Pod only while it runs
Infrequent changes where a scheduled refresh is acceptable
Continuous updates without a scheduled Job (the docs' recommendation)
when: Apps that read secrets from environment variables and must pick up rotated values.
Rotation in Secrets Manager should reach the Pods automatically, without a manual rollout.
A standalone Secrets Provider already keeps Kubernetes Secrets in sync across namespaces.
Teams that prefer a restart over changing code to re-read secrets.
diff: Availability
Same feature and same Helm values in SaaS and Self-Hosted.
What differs
Only how the Secrets Provider connects and authenticates (SaaS tenant vs Leader or Follower; Self-Hosted adds authn-k8s). Reloader itself never talks to Secrets Manager.
limits: Requires the Secrets Provider Helm chart in application or standalone mode. It does not apply to the init container or sidecar setups.
The docs cover Deployments and StatefulSets, and only when the Pod spec references the Secret directly (envFrom, secretKeyRef or volume).
Application mode needs an external trigger (for example a CronJob) to rerun the Job; without it the Secret never changes and nothing restarts.
Reloader always runs as a persistent Deployment, adding a running Pod even when the Provider is a short-lived Job.
Namespace-scoped by default. With a multi-namespace allowlist you must set watchGlobally: true or Helm rejects the install, and the wider scope needs a ClusterRole.
One replica by default: if it is down when a Secret changes, Pods keep the stale value until a manual restart or the next change. Enable HA where that matters.
Every change rolls the annotated workloads. In busy clusters, watch traffic and controller memory grow.

k8s_secretless.title: Secretless Broker
k8s_secretless.subtitle: The application connects to a local Secretless Broker with no credentials at all. Secretless fetches them from Secrets Manager, authenticates to the database or service on the app's behalf and then streams the traffic. The app never holds the secret.
k8s_secretless.flow_lead: Secretless runs as a sidecar in the application Pod and listens on a local socket. Follow a PostgreSQL connection, including a rotation.

flow.diagram_label: Diagram: the application connects to the Secretless sidecar without credentials; Secretless authenticates to the Follower, fetches the database password, authenticates to PostgreSQL and streams the traffic.
flow.s1_desc: The application opens a normal database connection to localhost:5432 (or a Unix socket), where Secretless listens. It sends no password, or a dummy one that Secretless replaces.
flow.s2_desc: Secretless authenticates to the Follower with the Kubernetes Authenticator (authn-k8s). The host identity comes from the Pod (namespace, service account), and the container must carry the name set in the host annotation, for example secretless.
flow.s3_desc: With its access token, Secretless retrieves the database credentials. They stay inside the Secretless process.
flow.s4_desc: Secretless opens the connection to PostgreSQL and performs the authentication phase of the protocol with the real credentials, over TLS to the database.
flow.s5_desc: After the handshake, Secretless pipes the data between the application and the database without changing it.
flow.s6_desc: When the password is rotated in Secrets Manager, Secretless picks up the new value and uses it for new connections. Nothing restarts.
flow.s7_desc: The application, its logs and its environment never contain the password, so a code bug, a log line or an environment dump cannot leak it.

k8s_secretless.roles_lead: Inside Secretless, each configured service gets a listener, a connector and one or more secret providers.
roles: Client application
Connects to Secretless as if it were the target; only knows where Secretless listens.
Secretless Broker (sidecar)
Local proxy in the same Pod; keeps the identity and the secrets inside its own process.
Listener (listenOn)
One socket per service: tcp://localhost:port or unix:///path.
Service connector
Speaks the target protocol and performs the authentication handshake (pg, mysql, mssql, ssh, ssh-agent, HTTP).
Secret provider
Where the credentials come from; in production, Secrets Manager (identifier conjur).
Configuration
secretless.yml (version 2) or a Kubernetes CRD listing each service, its connector and its credentials.
Follower + authn-k8s
Self-Hosted Follower in the cluster that authenticates the Secretless container and serves the secrets.
k8s_secretless.conn_lead: Secretless only brokers protocols it has a connector for.
conn: Database connector. The client may send dummy credentials; between client and Secretless, sslmode disable is the safest choice.
Database connector with the same model; TLS to the server (sslmode, sslrootcert) is set in Secretless.
SQL Server Authentication only, over TCP/IP only, with the limits of the go-mssqldb library.
Man in the middle that authenticates inbound SSH connections without exposing passwords or keys.
Replaces ssh-agent over a socket (SSH_AUTH_SOCK) without exposing keys.
Injects credentials into HTTP requests: Authorization header, AWS signature, or any header or query field.
k8s_secretless.prov_lead: Built-in sources Secretless can read credentials from.
prov: The production choice: authenticates with the workload identity and fetches variables.
Reads a Kubernetes Secret; the Pod needs read access to it.
Local sources. The docs recommend fetching from a vault in production.
caps: No code change
The app keeps its normal driver; only the connection URL (or a proxy setting) points to Secretless.
Rotation without restart
New connections use the new secret automatically.
Smaller threat surface
Leaks through logs, source control, environment dumps or app vulnerabilities cannot expose a secret the app never had.
Short-lived handling
HTTP and SSH credentials are fetched per connection and zeroized after the authentication.
Extensible
A connector plugin interface adds new protocols.
when: Apps that connect to supported databases, SSH or HTTP APIs and must never see the password.
Legacy apps you cannot change to call an SDK or read files.
Frequent rotation where restarts are not acceptable.
Kubernetes or OpenShift on Secrets Manager Self-Hosted, with a Follower in the cluster.
diff: Availability
Documented only for Secrets Manager Self-Hosted. The SaaS docs have no Secretless pages; on SaaS, use the Secrets Provider, the CSI driver or the SDKs.
Authentication
The Kubernetes sidecar guide uses authn-k8s with a Follower deployed in the cluster.
limits: Self-Hosted only: Secretless is not documented for Secrets Manager SaaS.
Only protocols with a connector work (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL, SSH, SSH agent, HTTP). A new protocol needs code, through the connector plugin interface.
HTTP: the client must call Secretless with plain http:// so Secretless can read the request; TLS runs from Secretless to the target. One HTTP backend per socket.
Generic HTTP cannot handle schemes that sign the request body with a secret key.
MSSQL: SQL Server Authentication only and TCP/IP only, plus the limits of go-mssqldb.
AWS: the client needs http_proxy pointing at Secretless, an http:// endpoint and dummy AWS credentials.
The channel to Secretless must not leave the Pod: over TCP, listen only on localhost; with Unix sockets, protect the file with OS permissions.
Kubernetes guide prerequisites: a Follower with the Kubernetes Authenticator in the cluster, a database that supports SSL, and the sidecar named as in the host annotation.

ci_terraform.title: Terraform and Secrets Manager
ci_terraform.subtitle: The open source Secrets Manager provider (terraform-provider-conjur) authenticates Terraform to Secrets Manager and reads secrets inside the manifest, so no password, key or token is hard coded in the .tf files.
ci_terraform.flow_title: How a pipeline gets a secret into Terraform
ci_terraform.flow_lead: Example with JWT authentication, the usual choice in a CI job. The provider also accepts API key, AWS IAM, Azure and GCP; the policy and fetch steps are the same.
ci_terraform.caps_lead: Configured in the Terraform manifest itself; access to every value is still decided by Secrets Manager policy.
caps: Read secrets
The conjur_secret data source (or its ephemeral form) fetches a variable by name and exposes it to the rest of the manifest.
Five authenticators
API key, AWS IAM, Azure, GCP and JWT (a valid JWT from a third party, such as the CI platform).
Sensitive values
Mark outputs with sensitive = true so the value never appears in the plan, in logs or on screen.
Keep secrets out of state
Ephemeral conjur_secret (Terraform 1.10+) and write-only secret arguments (Terraform 1.11+) avoid persisting values in the state file.
Manage Secrets Manager as code
Resources for policy branches, workloads (hosts), groups, memberships, permissions, secrets and authenticators.
Certificates (SaaS)
conjur_certificate_issue and conjur_certificate_sign data sources, with the Certificate Manager integration.
ci_terraform.roles_lead: Who does what when terraform plan or apply runs in a pipeline.
roles: terraform-provider-conjur
Plugin loaded by terraform init (Terraform Registry cyberark/conjur, binary, Homebrew or source). Authenticates and fetches.
provider "conjur" block
appliance_url, account, authn_type, service_id and the credential. Each field can come from CONJUR_* environment variables; the block wins when both exist.
Workload (host)
Identity that represents Terraform, with the chosen authenticator enabled for it.
Authenticator
authn (API key), authn-iam, authn-azure, authn-gcp or authn-jwt/{service-id}.
Policy
execute on each variable read; create or update on the parent policy for each resource Terraform manages.
Summon (Self-Hosted docs)
Alternative: summon terraform apply injects secrets as TF_VAR_name environment variables, listed in secrets.yml.
when: Infrastructure pipelines that need database passwords, cloud keys or certificates while creating resources.
You want to remove credentials from .tf files, terraform.tfvars and CI variables.
You want the Secrets Manager structure itself (branches, workloads, grants) versioned and reviewed as Terraform code.
Your team already uses Summon: the Self-Hosted docs describe summon terraform apply with no extra installation.
ci_terraform.diff_lead: Same provider and same manifest syntax; what changes is the endpoint, the identity paths and a few extras.
diff: Endpoint
SaaS: appliance_url is the API URL (https://<subdomain>.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api) and account is conjur. Self-Hosted: your own server URL and account name.
Identity paths
SaaS workloads live under data/ (for example data/repo-id). Self-Hosted examples use the path you defined (for example repo-id).
Certificate data sources
conjur_certificate_issue and conjur_certificate_sign are documented only for SaaS (Certificate Manager integration).
Managed resources
SaaS lists conjur_host and conjur_secret as resources too; the Self-Hosted page lists authenticator, policy branch, group, membership and permission.
Summon option
Documented only for Self-Hosted (Terraform with the Summon utility).
API key on workloads
SaaS: a workload that uses API key needs the annotation authn/api-key: true.
limits: Terraform stores data source values in the state file. Only the ephemeral form (Terraform 1.10+) or write-only arguments (Terraform 1.11+) keep a secret out of state: protect the state file anyway.
sensitive = true hides a value in output and logs, but does not stop it from being written to state.
Secrets Manager might reject concurrent changes under the same branch: if you see conflicts, run with -parallelism=1 and re-run terraform apply.
Nothing can be added to a policy branch before it exists or after it is destroyed: declare explicit dependencies (depends_on or attribute references).
Changes made outside Terraform (CLI, API, policy loads) cause state drift: always review terraform plan.
Never put sensitive fields such as api_key in the .tf file: use environment variables or Terraform sensitive variables.
Requires Terraform 0.13.0 or later; Go 1.25.3 or later only to compile from source. Supported on macOS, Linux and Windows.
In JWT mode, host_id is required when the authenticator does not define token-app-property and identity-path.
Summon (Self-Hosted): The documentation recommends the provider if you are not already familiar with Summon, and Summon must run on the same machine where authentication is configured.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a CI job runs Terraform with the Secrets Manager provider, authenticates with a JWT, reads a secret with execute permission and applies it without storing it in state.
flow.s1_desc: The job runs Terraform. The conjur provider block points to Secrets Manager and says how to authenticate; no secret is written in the manifest.
flow.s2_desc: Terraform installs cyberark/conjur. Fields such as appliance_url and account can come from CONJUR_* environment variables.
flow.s3_title: The CI platform issues a JWT
flow.s3_desc: The job receives a short-lived JWT from its platform and passes it to the provider as authn_jwt_token (or an environment variable).
flow.s4_desc: Secrets Manager checks the JWT signature against the issuer JWKS and validates the iss claim configured on the authenticator.
flow.s5_desc: token-app-property and identity-path turn a claim into the workload (host) ID. Secrets Manager returns a short-lived access token.
flow.s6_desc: The workload needs execute on the variable. Using the ephemeral form, the value lives only during the operation.
flow.s7_desc: The resource is created with the secret. Outputs marked sensitive stay hidden, and the ephemeral value is not written to the state file.

ci_gitlab.title: GitLab CI and Secrets Manager
ci_gitlab.subtitle: An official Docker image with a small Go binary authenticates the job with its GitLab ID token (JWT) and prints the requested secrets to STDOUT, so the pipeline needs no stored credential at all.
ci_gitlab.flow_title: How a GitLab job gets a secret
ci_gitlab.flow_lead: The job proves who it is with the JWT that GitLab mints for it. Secrets Manager trusts GitLab's public keys, maps a claim to a workload and checks the project and branch before releasing anything.
ci_gitlab.caps_lead: Works with GitLab Enterprise Edition and self-hosted GitLab.
caps: Secretless pipeline
No API key or password in CI/CD variables: the only credential is the job ID token, which GitLab issues per run.
Ready-made images
authn-jwt-gitlab for Alpine, Ubuntu and UBI-FIPS, used as the job image.
Claim-based identity
token-app-property (for example namespace_path) and identity-path map the JWT to a workload (host).
Project and branch pinning
Workload annotations such as authn-jwt/gitlab/project_path and authn-jwt/gitlab/ref restrict which project and ref can authenticate.
Policy per secret
The workload only reads variables it has execute on, including secrets synced from PAM Safes.
UI or policy as code
Authenticator and workload can be created in the UI (GitLab type) or with policy files and the CLI.
ci_gitlab.roles_lead: Pieces you configure on each side.
roles: id_tokens in .gitlab-ci.yml
Asks GitLab for an ID token (ID_TOKEN_1) whose aud must match the authenticator audience.
authn-jwt-gitlab image
Job image with the /authn-jwt-gitlab binary. It reads CONJUR_* variables, authenticates and prints the secret.
CONJUR_* variables
CONJUR_APPLIANCE_URL, CONJUR_ACCOUNT, CONJUR_AUTHN_JWT_SERVICE_ID (gitlab, without authn-jwt/), CONJUR_AUTHN_JWT_TOKEN and CONJUR_SECRET_ID.
JWT authenticator
authn-jwt/gitlab with jwks-uri (https://gitlab.com/oauth/discovery/keys), issuer, audience, token-app-property and identity-path.
Workload (host)
For example data/gitlab-apps/namespace1, member of the authenticator apps group, with ref and project_path annotations.
GitLab Runner
Docker runner that executes the job; self-hosted GitLab and Runner setup scripts are in the docs.
when: GitLab pipelines that deploy, migrate databases or call APIs and today keep credentials in masked CI/CD variables.
You want access tied to the project and branch, not to a long-lived key that anyone with maintainer access can read.
Self-hosted GitLab or GitLab EE: both are supported.
You need a single audit trail of which pipeline read which secret.
ci_gitlab.diff_lead: The image, the variables and the JWT logic are the same; the differences are in the endpoint and in how the authenticator is enabled.
diff: Endpoint and account
SaaS: CONJUR_APPLIANCE_URL is https://<subdomain>.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api and CONJUR_ACCOUNT must be conjur. Self-Hosted: your server URL and account name.
Self-signed certificate
Self-Hosted adds CONJUR_SSL_CERTIFICATE or CONJUR_CERT_FILE when the server uses a self-signed certificate.
Creating the authenticator

SaaS: UI wizard (JSON Web Token, GitLab type) or CLI; requires Authn_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Admins. Self-Hosted: policy loaded into root with the CLI, then the authenticator must be allowlisted (enabled) on the server.
Workload paths
SaaS workloads live under data/ (data/gitlab-apps). Secret IDs follow, for example data/vault/<safe>/<secret>.
Self-hosted GitLab
Use your GitLab URL (for example http://gitlab.example.com:9080) for jwks-uri and issuer instead of https://gitlab.com.
limits: Requires Docker, Go 1.20.2 or later, GitLab on Docker 15.11.2 or later, GitLab Runner on Docker 15.8.2 or later and the Secrets Manager CLI v9.x.
Images are available only for Alpine, Ubuntu and UBI-FIPS.
The binary returns each secret to STDOUT: one call per CONJUR_SECRET_ID, captured into a variable by the job script.
The ID token aud must exactly match the authenticator audience variable, or authentication fails.
CONJUR_AUTHN_JWT_SERVICE_ID takes only the authenticator name (gitlab), not authn-jwt/gitlab.
SaaS: CONJUR_ACCOUNT must be conjur.
Creating the JWT authenticator requires admin rights (create on the authn-jwt policy, through Authn_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Admins).
The policies in the docs are samples only: adapt them to your environment.
