flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a GitLab job gets an ID token, the authn-jwt-gitlab binary authenticates to Secrets Manager, which checks GitLab's JWKS, the workload and its annotations, then the secret is printed to STDOUT and used in the deploy.
flow.s1_desc: A GitLab job runs on the authn-jwt-gitlab image. It holds no stored credential; GitLab will vouch for it.
flow.s2_desc: id_tokens in .gitlab-ci.yml asks for ID_TOKEN_1 with aud conjur. The job passes it in CONJUR_AUTHN_JWT_TOKEN.
flow.s3_desc: /authn-jwt-gitlab posts the JWT to the authenticator named in CONJUR_AUTHN_JWT_SERVICE_ID (gitlab).
flow.s4_desc: Secrets Manager validates the signature with GitLab's JWKS (/oauth/discovery/keys) and checks iss and aud against the authenticator.
flow.s5_desc: namespace_path (namespace1) under identity-path data/gitlab-apps gives the workload. Its annotations require ref master and project_path namespace1/jwt-example.
flow.s6_desc: Every check passed, so Secrets Manager returns an access token to the binary.
flow.s7_desc: For each CONJUR_SECRET_ID the workload needs execute. The value goes to STDOUT and the script captures it, for example export DB_PASS=$(...).
flow.s8_desc: Later script lines use the variable to deploy. Nothing was stored in GitLab settings.

ci_azdo.title: Azure DevOps and Secrets Manager
ci_azdo.subtitle: The Idira Conjur Service Connector is an Azure DevOps extension that authenticates the pipeline to Secrets Manager and fetches a batch of secrets into environment variables. JWT through an Azure identity is recommended; API key is also supported.
ci_azdo.flow_title: How an Azure pipeline gets its secrets
ci_azdo.flow_lead: JWT mode: the pipeline borrows an Entra ID token from an Azure Resource Manager service connection, so no Secrets Manager credential is stored in Azure DevOps.
ci_azdo.caps_lead: Installed from the Visual Studio Marketplace into your Azure DevOps organization.
caps: Batch retrieval
Every secret listed in a secrets.yml file is fetched in one go and assigned to the pipeline environment variable you name.
JWT with an Azure identity
Uses a managed identity or an app registration through an Azure Resource Manager service connection. Recommended.
API key option
Conjur Batch Secrets Server Connection with a workload ID and its API key, when JWT is not possible.
Claim mapping
token-app-property (for example sub, the identity Object ID) names the workload; an annotation such as appid pins the client.
Classic or YAML
Add the Conjur Secret Retrieval Connector task from the Tasks panel or as a YAML step.
Troubleshooting path
System diagnostics plus a documented AzureCLI pipeline to dump and decode the JWT on a 401.
ci_azdo.roles_lead: Pieces on the Azure, Azure DevOps and Secrets Manager sides.
roles: Managed identity or app registration
Azure identity whose token authenticates. Client ID is the token appid; Object ID is the token sub.
Azure Resource Manager service connection
JWT only: generates the Entra ID token for that identity inside the pipeline.
Conjur JWT Batch Secrets Server Connection
Service connection with the Secrets Manager URL, account, Service ID (authenticator name without authn-jwt/) and optional Host ID.
Conjur Batch Secrets Server Connection
API key mode: URL, account, Username (host/<workload path>) and the workload API key.
secrets.yml
File in the triggering repo: ENV_VAR: !var <secret id>, one line per secret.
authn-jwt/azure-devops
jwks-uri https://login.windows.net/common/discovery/keys, issuer https://sts.windows.net/<tenant-id>/, identity-path and token-app-property.
when: Azure Pipelines that deploy to Azure or elsewhere and keep secrets in variable groups or pipeline variables today.
You already run a managed identity or app registration for the pipeline and want Secrets Manager to trust it.
You want one place (Secrets Manager policy) to decide which pipeline reads which secret, with audit.
Read-only consumption is enough: the extension does not write secrets.
ci_azdo.diff_lead: Same extension and same service connection types; the differences are the endpoint, the account and how the authenticator is enabled.
diff: Endpoint
SaaS: the API endpoint https://<subdomain>.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api. Self-Hosted: your server URL (for example https://acme.conjur.com).
Account name
SaaS: must be conjur. Self-Hosted: your Secrets Manager account name.
Workload IDs
SaaS: host/data/<workload>. Self-Hosted: host/<workload> in the path you defined.
CA certificate
SaaS: generally not required. Self-Hosted: required when the server uses a self-signed certificate.
Enabling the authenticator
SaaS: CLI command to enable it. Self-Hosted: add authn-jwt/azure-devops to the authenticators list in conjur.yml on the server and apply the change.
limits: The Idira Conjur Service Connector does not support creating, updating or removing secrets.
JWT mode needs an Azure identity (managed identity or app registration) and an Azure Resource Manager service connection.
The pipeline must be able to read secrets.yml: keep the file in the repository that triggers the pipeline.
Host ID is required only when the JWT authenticator does not define token-app-property and identity-path.
Service ID takes the authenticator name only (azure-devops), not authn-jwt/azure-devops.
SaaS: Conjur Account Name must be conjur.
On a 401, the documented check is to dump the JWT with an AzureCLI job, decode it twice and compare issuer, identity-path, token-app-property, jwks-uri, workload ID and annotation.
ci_azdo.limits_source: Source: Secrets Manager docs, Azure DevOps (Limitations)
ci_azdo.doc_marketplace: Idira Conjur Service Connector on the Marketplace

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: an Azure pipeline reads secrets.yml, gets an Entra ID token through its service connection, authenticates to Secrets Manager, which checks the JWKS, the workload and the appid annotation, then fetches all secrets in one batch into environment variables.
flow.s1_desc: A pipeline runs the Conjur Secret Retrieval Connector task with the Conjur JWT Batch Secrets Server Connection.
flow.s2_desc: The task reads the file from the repo: each line maps a pipeline environment variable to a secret ID.
flow.s3_desc: The Azure Resource Manager service connection gets a JWT for the managed identity or app registration.
flow.s4_desc: The task sends the JWT to authn-jwt/azure-devops. Secrets Manager checks the signature with the login.windows.net JWKS and the sts.windows.net issuer.
flow.s5_desc: The sub claim, under identity-path, is the workload ID; the appid annotation must match. Secrets Manager returns an access token.
flow.s6_desc: With execute on every listed variable, the values come back in one batch and become pipeline environment variables.
flow.s7_desc: Following tasks read the environment variables to deploy. No Secrets Manager credential was stored in Azure DevOps.

ci_bitbucket.title: Bitbucket Pipelines: secrets through the Bitbucket Pipe
ci_bitbucket.subtitle: A pipeline step with OIDC enabled proves who it is with a Bitbucket-signed JWT. The Bitbucket Pipe trades that token at the JWT authenticator, fetches only the secrets you list and hands them to the rest of the step. No API key is stored in Bitbucket.
ci_bitbucket.flow_title: How a pipeline step gets its secrets
ci_bitbucket.flow_lead: Play the steps: OIDC token, JWT authenticator, workload match by repository UUID, then the .secrets folder and load_secrets.sh.
caps: Authenticates with the Bitbucket OIDC token of the step (oidc: true), so no long-lived credential is kept in repository variables.
Maps the repositoryUuid claim to a workload (host) named after the repository UUID, so each repository gets its own identity and its own grants.
Fetches a comma-separated list of secret IDs in one pipe call.
Writes the values to .secrets/secrets.env (dotenv format, key = last part of the secret ID, for example secret1).
Ships load_secrets.sh, which exports the values into the shell and deletes secrets.env right after.
Works with secrets synced from PAM Safes: grant the workload the Safe's consumers group.
ci_bitbucket.how_lead: Who does what between Bitbucket and Secrets Manager.
roles: Bitbucket OIDC provider
Signs a JWT for the step. Issuer: https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/workspaces/{workspace}/pipelines-config/identity/oidc; keys at …/oidc/keys.json.
Pipeline step (oidc: true)
Runs the pipe cyberark-conjur/conjur-bitbucket-pipe inside the step and receives the OIDC token.
JWT authenticator authn-jwt/bitbucket
Validates signature and issuer, reads token-app-property = repositoryUuid and looks for the workload under identity-path data/bitbucket-pipes.
Workload (host) {repositoryUuid}
Named after the repository UUID, annotated authn-jwt/bitbucket/repositoryUuid, member of the authenticator's apps group.
Secret consumer groups
Grant read access, for example vault/{safe}/delegation/consumers for secrets synced from PAM.
.secrets folder
secrets.env with the values and load_secrets.sh to export them and delete the file.
ci_bitbucket.fields_lead: What goes under variables: in bitbucket-pipelines.yml.
fields: SaaS: the API URL, https://{subdomain}.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api. Self-Hosted: your Secrets Manager server URL.
SaaS: if set, must be conjur. Self-Hosted: your account name, defaults to conjur.
Name of the JWT authenticator, for example bitbucket.
when: Your code lives in Bitbucket Cloud and pipelines need database, API or cloud credentials.
You want to remove secured repository variables and long-lived API keys from Bitbucket.
You want one identity per repository, auditable in Secrets Manager.
The credentials already live in PAM Safes and are synced to Secrets Manager.
diff: Creating the authenticator: SaaS through the UI (JSON Web Token, Other), the CLI (policy loaded into conjur/authn-jwt) or the APIv2. Self-Hosted: policy with id conjur/authn-jwt/bitbucket loaded at root.
Discovery: SaaS sets jwks-uri plus issuer. The Self-Hosted guide sets provider-uri (the Bitbucket OIDC URL) instead.
Enabling: SaaS runs conjur authenticator enable --id authn-jwt/bitbucket. Self-Hosted adds authn-jwt/bitbucket to the authenticators list in conjur.yml and runs evoke configuration apply.
Workload: SaaS offers a Bitbucket workload type in the UI and Access to Safes for PAM-synced secrets. Self-Hosted defines the host and its grant in policy.
Pipe variables: SaaS uses the /api URL and account conjur. Self-Hosted uses the server URL and your account name.
limits: Secrets are written to a subdirectory of the current working directory in the container. Every process in the pipeline step can read it, so be careful not to expose secrets to unauthorized processes.
Because of the .env file format, secrets with special characters other than _ are not supported, and variable names cannot start with a number.
If you load secrets.env yourself instead of using load_secrets.sh, you must delete the file afterwards.
Requires a Bitbucket Cloud repository and a step with oidc: true.
The workload name and its annotation must be the repository UUID, braces included, exactly as shown in Repository settings, OpenID Connect.
On SaaS, CONJUR_ACCOUNT, when set, must be conjur.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a Bitbucket pipeline step authenticates to IDIRA Secrets Manager with its OIDC token and receives secrets in the .secrets folder.
flow.s1_desc: A Bitbucket pipeline step, the Bitbucket OIDC provider and IDIRA Secrets Manager. Nothing secret is stored in the repository.
flow.s2_desc: With oidc: true, Bitbucket signs a JWT for the step. Claims include iss (workspace), repositoryUuid, branchName and stepUuid.
flow.s3_desc: conjur-bitbucket-pipe posts the token to the authenticator named in CONJUR_SERVICE_ID (bitbucket).
flow.s4_desc: Secrets Manager validates the signature with the workspace keys.json and compares iss with the configured issuer.
flow.s5_desc: token-app-property = repositoryUuid: the claim value names the workload under data/bitbucket-pipes. Its annotation must match and it must be in the apps group.
flow.s6_desc: Secrets Manager returns an access token for that workload only.
flow.s7_desc: The pipe reads each ID in SECRETS. Policy decides: the workload needs read access, for example through a Safe's consumers group.
flow.s8_desc: The pipe writes secrets.env (dotenv, key = last part of the ID). Any process in the step can read this folder.
flow.s9_desc: load_secrets.sh exports the values into the shell and deletes secrets.env. Later scripts in the step use them to reach the target.

ci_circleci.title: CircleCI: secrets through the orb
ci_circleci.subtitle: Each CircleCI job can get an OIDC token signed by your organization. The orb trades it at the JWT authenticator and exports the secrets you list as environment variables for the job. No API key lives in CircleCI.
ci_circleci.flow_title: How a job gets its secrets
ci_circleci.flow_lead: Play the steps: OIDC token, JWT authenticator with audience, workload match by project and sub, then environment variables.
caps: Authenticates with the job's CircleCI OIDC token, so no long-lived credential is stored in CircleCI.
Checks the audience: aud must be your CircleCI organization ID.
Maps oidc.circleci.com/project-id to a workload named after the project ID, and the workload's sub annotation pins organization, project, user, repository and ref.
Fetches a semicolon-separated list of secret IDs with the retrieve_secret job step.
Exports each value as an environment variable named after the last part of the secret ID, or a custom name with the | syntax.
Accepts a PEM certificate when Secrets Manager uses a self-signed certificate.
The connection fields can live in a CircleCI context instead of the config file.
ci_circleci.how_lead: Who does what between CircleCI and Secrets Manager.
roles: CircleCI OIDC provider
Signs the job token. Issuer: https://oidc.circleci.com/org/{org-id}; keys at …/.well-known/jwks-pub.json.
CircleCI job
Uses the orb cyberark/conjur-circleci-orb and its retrieve_secret step.
JWT authenticator authn-jwt/circle-ci
Validates signature, issuer and audience, reads token-app-property = oidc.circleci.com/project-id, identity-path data/circleci-apps.
Workload (host) {project-id}
Named after the project ID, annotated authn-jwt/circle-ci/sub with the full sub claim, member of the apps group.
Secret consumer groups
Grant read access, for example vault/{safe}/delegation/consumers for PAM-synced secrets.
Job environment
Receives one environment variable per secret.
ci_circleci.fields_lead: What the orb step needs in .circleci/config.yml (or in a context).
fields: SaaS: the API URL, https://{subdomain}.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api. Self-Hosted: your Secrets Manager server URL.
SaaS: must be conjur. Self-Hosted: your account name.
Name of the JWT authenticator, for example circle-ci.
Server certificate in PEM, when Secrets Manager uses a self-signed certificate.
Semicolon-separated secret IDs. Add |name to choose the variable, for example data/circleci-apps/secret1|DB_USER.
when: Your pipelines run on CircleCI and need credentials for deploys, tests or cloud APIs.
You want to stop storing secrets in CircleCI project settings or contexts.
You want access tied to a specific project, repository and branch.
The credentials already live in PAM Safes and are synced to Secrets Manager.
diff: Creating the authenticator: SaaS through the UI (JSON Web Token, Other), the CLI (policy loaded into conjur/authn-jwt) or the APIv2. Self-Hosted: policy loaded at root, then variables set with the CLI.
Enabling: SaaS runs conjur authenticator enable --id authn-jwt/circle-ci. Self-Hosted adds authn-jwt/circle-ci to conjur.yml and runs evoke configuration apply.
Identity path: the SaaS example uses data/circleci-apps. The Self-Hosted example uses circleci-apps.
Workload: SaaS offers Access to Safes for PAM-synced secrets in the UI. Self-Hosted defines the host in policy.
Orb fields: SaaS uses the /api URL and account conjur. Self-Hosted uses the server URL and your account name.
limits: The CircleCI guide has no Limitations section. The items below are requirements stated in the guide.

The workload's sub annotation holds the full sub claim: organization, project, user, repository and ref. A run started by another user or from another branch carries a different sub and will not match that workload.
The audience must be set to your CircleCI organization ID.
On SaaS, account must be conjur.
If Secrets Manager uses a self-signed certificate, you must pass it in PEM through the certificate field.
secrets is a semicolon-separated list. Without a custom name (|name), the variable takes the last part of the secret ID.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a CircleCI job authenticates to IDIRA Secrets Manager with its OIDC token and receives secrets as environment variables.
flow.s1_desc: A CircleCI job, the CircleCI OIDC provider for your organization and IDIRA Secrets Manager.
flow.s2_desc: CircleCI signs a JWT for the job. aud is the organization ID; sub joins org, project, user, vcs-origin and vcs-ref.
flow.s3_desc: retrieve_secret posts the token to the authenticator named in service_id (circle-ci).
flow.s4_desc: Secrets Manager validates the signature with jwks-pub.json and checks iss and aud against the configured values.
flow.s5_desc: token-app-property = oidc.circleci.com/project-id names the workload under data/circleci-apps; its sub annotation must equal the token's sub.
flow.s6_desc: Secrets Manager returns an access token for that workload only.
flow.s7_desc: The orb reads each ID in secrets. The workload needs read access, for example through a Safe's consumers group.
flow.s8_desc: Each value is exported as an environment variable: the last part of the ID, or the name after |.
flow.s9_desc: Later steps of the job read the variables to reach the target. Nothing was stored in CircleCI settings.

ci_octopus.title: Octopus Deploy: secrets through a step template
ci_octopus.subtitle: Octopus signs a JWT through a Generic OIDC account. The step template CyberArk Secrets Manager, Retrieve Secrets (JWT) trades it at the JWT authenticator and publishes each secret as an output variable for the next deployment steps. Works with Octopus Cloud and self-hosted Octopus.
ci_octopus.flow_title: How a deployment gets its secrets
ci_octopus.flow_lead: Play the steps: Generic OIDC account, JWT authenticator, workload match by sub, then output variables for later steps.
caps: Uses Octopus native OpenID Connect: a Generic OIDC account with audience conjur, referenced by a project variable.
Builds the sub claim from the values you pick (recommended: space, project, environment), so each project and environment can be its own workload.
Fetches a multi-line list of secret IDs, each with an optional custom output name (secret-id | name).
Publishes the values as output variables of the step for later steps (PowerShell, Bash, Python examples in the guide).
Accepts a trusted server certificate in PEM for a self-signed Secrets Manager.
Can log the output variable names (Print Output Variable Names), disabled by default.
ci_octopus.how_lead: Who does what between Octopus and Secrets Manager.
roles: Octopus OIDC (Generic OIDC account)
Issuer https://{company}.octopus.app, keys at /.well-known/jwks, audience conjur. sub looks like space:default:project:get-secrets:environment:development.
Project variable
References the OIDC account; the step reads it through CyberArk.SecretsManager.Jwt.
Step template Retrieve Secrets (JWT)
Community step template that posts the JWT and fetches the secrets.
JWT authenticator authn-jwt/octopus
Validates signature, issuer and audience, token-app-property = sub, identity-path data/octopus-apps.
Workload (host) {sub}
Named after the sub value, annotated authn-jwt/octopus/sub, member of the apps group.
Output variables
Octopus.Action[...].Output.{name} for the following steps.
ci_octopus.fields_lead: Parameters of CyberArk Secrets Manager, Retrieve Secrets (JWT).
fields: CyberArk.SecretsManager.Account. SaaS: if set, must be conjur. Self-Hosted: your account name, defaults to conjur.
CyberArk.SecretsManager.Url. SaaS: https://{subdomain}.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api. Self-Hosted: your server URL.
CyberArk.SecretsManager.ServiceId. Name of the JWT authenticator, default octopus.
CyberArk.SecretsManager.Jwt. The project variable that references the Generic OIDC account.
CyberArk.SecretsManager.Variables. One per line: secret-id | output-name. Without a name, the secret ID is the output name.
CyberArk.SecretsManager.Certificate. PEM certificate, for example for a self-signed server.
CyberArk.SecretsManager.PrintVariableNames. Logs the names, disabled by default.
when: Your releases and runbooks run in Octopus Deploy (Cloud or self-hosted).
You want per-environment access: development and production deployments of the same project get different workloads.
You want to stop keeping credentials as Octopus sensitive variables.
The credentials already live in PAM Safes and are synced to Secrets Manager.
diff: Creating the authenticator: SaaS through the UI (JSON Web Token, Other), the CLI (policy loaded into conjur/authn-jwt) or the APIv2. Self-Hosted: policy loaded at root, variables set with the CLI.
Enabling: SaaS runs conjur authenticator enable --id authn-jwt/octopus. Self-Hosted adds authn-jwt/octopus to conjur.yml and runs evoke configuration apply.
Workload: SaaS offers an Octopus Deploy workload type and Access to Safes in the UI. Self-Hosted defines the host in policy.
Step parameters: SaaS uses the /api URL and account conjur. Self-Hosted uses the server URL and your account name.
Failure behaviour: only the SaaS guide states that one missing or inaccessible secret fails the whole step.
limits: If several secrets are mapped to the same custom variable, the last one wins and the previous values are overwritten.
If one secret is inaccessible or does not exist, the step fails and no secrets are retrieved (stated in the SaaS guide).
The workload name and its sub annotation must equal the sub claim, which depends on the values chosen in the Generic OIDC account (space, project, environment are recommended).
The Generic OIDC account audience must be conjur, matching the authenticator's audience.
On SaaS, Secrets Manager Account, when set, must be conjur.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: an Octopus deployment authenticates to IDIRA Secrets Manager with a Generic OIDC token and publishes secrets as output variables.
flow.s1_desc: An Octopus deployment or runbook, the Octopus server acting as OIDC issuer and IDIRA Secrets Manager.
flow.s2_desc: The Generic OIDC account signs a token with aud conjur and a sub built from space, project and environment.
flow.s3_desc: The step template posts the token to the authenticator in Authenticator Service ID (octopus by default).
flow.s4_desc: Secrets Manager validates the signature with the Octopus /.well-known/jwks keys and checks iss and aud.
flow.s5_desc: token-app-property = sub: the value, for example space:default:project:get-secrets:environment:development, names the workload under data/octopus-apps.
flow.s6_desc: Secrets Manager returns an access token for that workload only.
flow.s7_desc: The step reads each line of Secrets Manager Variables. If one is missing or not allowed, the step fails and returns nothing.
flow.s8_desc: Each value is published as an output variable: the custom name, or the secret ID. Same name twice: the last one wins.
flow.s9_desc: Later steps read Octopus.Action[...].Output.{name} to reach the target.

pf_python.title: Python: SDK and AWS IAM client
pf_python.subtitle: Two official ways for Python code to read secrets: the general Python SDK (conjur-api) and the AWS IAM client for Python, which lets an EC2 instance authenticate with its own IAM role, with no stored credential.
pf_python.flow_title: How the AWS IAM client gets a secret
pf_python.flow_lead: The script never holds a password. It signs a request with the role that AWS gave the instance, and Secrets Manager checks that signature with AWS STS.
pf_python.how_lead: The pieces you install, configure and call.
roles: conjur-api (Python SDK)
General client: login, get, get_many, set, policy load/replace/update, list, Host Factory, API key rotation. Installed with pip3 install conjur-api. Python 3.10 or later.
Credentials provider
Holds the login data and hands it to the client only when needed. SimpleCredentialsProvider for tests, or your own CredentialsProviderInterface (for example a keyring).
Authentication strategy
Keeps the login logic apart from the client: AuthnAuthenticationStrategy on both platforms; LdapAuthenticationStrategy and JWTAuthenticationStrategy on Self-Hosted.
conjur_iam_client (AWS IAM client)
create_conjur_iam_api_key builds the signed STS header; get_conjur_iam_session_token exchanges it for an access token; create_conjur_iam_client returns a ready Python client.
IAM authenticator (authn-iam)
Validates the signed request with AWS STS and matches AccountID/RoleName to the workload ID host/.../{aws-account-id}/{iam-role-name}.
Policy
Grants the workload read and execute on the secrets. Without a grant, a valid identity still gets nothing.
when: Python code on EC2 that should not carry any secret zero: the IAM role is the identity.
Scripts and services that need more than reading: loading policy, creating hosts with Host Factory or rotating API keys (Python SDK).
Self-Hosted estates that already use LDAP or a JWT issuer and want Python to authenticate the same way.
Automation that reads many secrets at once: get_many returns a dictionary in one call.
diff: Python SDK on SaaS: only Authn (API key) authentication is documented.
Python SDK on Self-Hosted: Authn, LDAP and JWT strategies; LDAP and JWT need the authenticator service_id in ConjurConnectionInfo.
AWS IAM client: same flow on both. On SaaS the workload lives under data/ and cert_file can be None; on Self-Hosted you pass the server CA file.
whoami() needs Secrets Manager v1.9 or later on Self-Hosted.
limits: The AWS IAM client cannot delete or update secrets: it is read only.
The client from create_conjur_iam_client does not refresh its token. It works for five to eight minutes; after that you must call the function again.
The AWS IAM client is installed from the GitHub source (git clone + pip3 install), not from a release on PyPI.
Python 3.10 or later is required for both libraries.
SimpleCredentialsProvider keeps credentials in process memory; for production, implement CredentialsProviderInterface with a proper store.
On SaaS the SDK documents only API key authentication: an API key is a secret zero that must be protected and rotated.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a Python script on EC2 uses its IAM role to get a Secrets Manager token and read a secret
flow.s1_desc: The AWS IAM client for Python wraps the Python SDK. The script runs on EC2 with an IAM role, and that role is the only proof of identity it needs.
flow.s2_desc: The client reads the temporary role credentials from the EC2 instance metadata. Nothing is stored on disk or in the code.
flow.s3_desc: create_conjur_iam_api_key builds a JSON header with an AWS SigV4 signature for sts:GetCallerIdentity. This header replaces the API key.
flow.s4_desc: get_conjur_iam_session_token posts the header to authn-iam. Secrets Manager replays it to AWS STS and compares the returned account and role with the workload ID.
flow.s5_desc: On a match, Secrets Manager returns an access token and create_conjur_iam_client returns a ready Python client built on that token.
flow.s6_desc: client.get(id) asks for the variable. Policy must grant the workload read and execute; the value comes back as bytes and stays in memory.
flow.s7_desc: The client does not refresh its token. After five to eight minutes requests fail, so the script calls create_conjur_iam_client again and repeats the signed login.

pf_cf.title: Cloud Foundry and VMware Tanzu
pf_cf.subtitle: A Service Broker gives every Cloud Foundry application its own identity in Secrets Manager, and a buildpack injects the secrets into the app environment at start. Documented for Self-Hosted only.
pf_cf.flow_title: From cf push to a database login
pf_cf.flow_lead: The developer never sees an API key. Binding the app to the service creates its identity; the buildpack uses it at start-up.
pf_cf.how_lead: The parts of the integration and what each one owns.
roles: Service Broker (tile)
Registers the cyberark-conjur service with the community plan in the Marketplace. Adds and removes host identities in its policy branch as apps are bound and unbound.
Service instance
One per space (cf create-service). Creates org and space groups in Secrets Manager, named by their GUIDs, so you can entitle a whole org or space.
Binding
cf bind-service (or the manifest) creates a host whose ID is the binding ID. The login appears as authn_login in VCAP_SERVICES.
Buildpack (conjur_buildpack)
Runs Summon at app start: reads secrets.yml, fetches each !var with the bound identity and puts the values in the process environment (or a temp file with !var:file).
Broker host
The Secrets Manager host the tile logs in with. Needs create and update on the dedicated policy branch (or on root if there is none).
Policy
Grants read and execute to the org, space or app host. Secrets are best kept in a branch outside the one the broker manages.
when: Applications on Tanzu Application Service or open source Cloud Foundry that should get secrets without a credential in the manifest.
Teams that want least privilege per org, per space or per application.
Apps that read configuration from environment variables: Summon fills them, no code change.
Concourse pipelines on Tanzu: Concourse supports Secrets Manager natively as a credential manager.
diff: App-scoped (default): one host per bound app. Each bind talks to the Leader.
Space-scoped (Enable Space-scoped App Identities): one host per space, shared by every app. Binding only needs a Follower, which helps availability and scale.
With space-scoped identities, grant access only to the org and space groups: individual apps cannot be entitled.
Tile versions before 1.5.0 used layers instead of groups for org and space.
limits: Documented for Secrets Manager Self-Hosted only. There is no SaaS page for Cloud Foundry or Tanzu.
Each space needs its own service instance: instances cannot be shared across spaces.
Without a dedicated policy branch, the broker host needs create and update on root, which lets it edit any policy.
Secrets are fetched once at start-up. A rotated value reaches the app only after a restart or restage.
Rotating an app-scoped API key means unbind and bind: that issues a new identity, so app-specific grants must be given again.
Rotating a space host key means updating the key in Secrets Manager, then rebinding and restaging every app in the space.
Compatibility: Ops Manager v2.7 to v3.0, TAS v4, v5, v6 and 10.2. Multiple buildpacks need cf CLI newer than 6.38.
docs: Install and configure the Service Broker

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: the Service Broker creates an identity for a Cloud Foundry app and the buildpack fetches its secrets at start
flow.s1_desc: The Service Broker manages identities; the buildpack uses them. Both talk to a Self-Hosted Secrets Manager, which can live outside Cloud Foundry.
flow.s2_title: Create the service in the space
flow.s2_desc: cf create-service cyberark-conjur community creates one instance in the space. The broker adds groups for the org and the space, named by their GUIDs.
flow.s3_desc: When the app is pushed and bound, the broker creates a host whose ID is the binding ID and adds it to the org and space groups.
flow.s4_desc: The binding credentials, including authn_login, reach the app in VCAP_SERVICES. They are visible only to the app, not to other users.
flow.s5_desc: The buildpack runs Summon, which reads secrets.yml and authenticates with the bound identity. Policy checks the grants on each !var.
flow.s6_desc: The values are injected into the app process environment only, and disappear when the process exits. !var:file writes a temp file instead.
flow.s7_desc: The app reads DB_PASSWORD from its environment and logs in. No secret was ever written to the manifest or the repository.

pf_puppet.title: Puppet
pf_puppet.subtitle: An official Puppet module configures workload identity at scale: each node gets its own Secrets Manager identity and fetches secrets with it, instead of having them compiled into the catalog. Documented for Self-Hosted only.
pf_puppet.flow_title: How a node gets a secret during a Puppet run
pf_puppet.flow_lead: The catalog carries a deferred call, not the value. The agent resolves it with its own identity at apply time.
pf_puppet.how_lead: The page in the documentation is short and points to the module README; these are the moving parts.
roles: Puppet module
Open source, hosted on GitHub and published to the Puppet Forge. Configures the workload so it can make authenticated calls to Secrets Manager.
Puppet Server
Compiles the catalog. With a Deferred function the secret is not resolved on the server, so it does not land in the catalog or in reports.
Puppet agent (node)
Holds the node identity (a host and its API key), authenticates to Secrets Manager and fetches the secret when the catalog is applied.
Secrets Manager host
One identity per node or per group of nodes, declared in policy like any other workload.
Policy
Grants the node host read and execute on the variables it needs.
when: Estates already managed by Puppet that need to place passwords, keys or certificates in configuration files and services.
Removing secrets from Hiera data, manifests and the compiled catalog.
Giving every node its own identity so access can be granted and revoked per node.
Linux and Windows fleets configured the same way at scale.
pf_puppet.diff_title: What to know before you start
diff: The documentation page is a pointer: the module README on GitHub is the full reference (parameters, identity setup, examples).
Deferred functions, which let the agent fetch at apply time, need Puppet 6 or later.
The node identity is an API key: protect it on disk and rotate it like any other secret zero.
The module is open source, so check its supported Puppet and OS versions in the README before rollout.
limits: Documented for Secrets Manager Self-Hosted only. There is no SaaS page for Puppet.
The official page gives no feature matrix; all details live in the module documentation on GitHub.
Authentication uses a host API key on the node: anyone who copies it can authenticate until it is rotated.
A secret resolved on the server instead of with Deferred ends up in the catalog, PuppetDB and reports.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a Puppet agent uses its own identity to fetch a secret at apply time
flow.s1_title: The node has its own identity
flow.s1_desc: With the Puppet module, every node is a workload in Secrets Manager. The server orchestrates, but the node is the one that asks for secrets.
flow.s2_desc: The node is configured once with its host ID and API key. From then on it can make authenticated calls on its own.
flow.s3_desc: Puppet Server compiles a catalog where the secret is a Deferred call. What travels to the agent is the instruction, not the password.
flow.s4_desc: At apply time the agent sends its API key to the authn endpoint and receives a short-lived access token.
flow.s5_desc: The deferred function asks for the variable. Policy checks the node grant and the value comes back only to that agent.
flow.s6_desc: The agent writes the file or configures the service with the value. The secret never sat in the catalog, PuppetDB or Hiera.

pf_mulesoft.title: MuleSoft Connector
pf_mulesoft.subtitle: A Mule connector that retrieves secrets from Secrets Manager inside a flow, so Mule applications stop carrying passwords for the systems they integrate. It authenticates with a workload API key.
pf_mulesoft.flow_title: How a Mule flow gets its secrets
pf_mulesoft.flow_lead: The Retrieve secret operation runs inside the flow: authenticate, ask for a list of secrets, pass the values to the next step.
pf_mulesoft.how_lead: What you add to the Mule project and what you set up in Secrets Manager.
roles: conjur-mule-connector
Mule plugin (Maven Central or built from GitHub) that adds the Retrieve secret operation (ConjurVaultConnector).
Connection properties
Account, Secrets Manager URL, workload ID, workload API key and, for Edge or Self-Hosted, the SSL certificate (.pem) or cert file (.der).
Secure properties
Placeholders such as ${secure::conjur.*} in a conjur.properties file keep the API key out of the configuration XML.
Workload (host)
Declared with authn/api-key: true on SaaS (or created on the Workloads page). Its API key is the connector login.
Policy
Grants the workload the Safe consumers group, for example delegation/consumers under data/vault/{safe}.
when: Mule applications that call databases, APIs or SaaS systems and today keep those credentials in properties files.
Secrets that live in a PAM Safe and are synced to Secrets Manager.
Teams that build in Anypoint Studio and want a drag-and-drop operation instead of REST calls.
Fetching several secrets in one operation (comma-separated key list).
diff: SaaS: account is conjur, the URL is https://{subdomain}.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud, the workload lives under data/ and secret IDs start with data/vault/.
SaaS: the SSL certificate or cert file is needed only when connecting to an Edge.
Self-Hosted: account is the one set at deployment, the host is loaded in root, secret IDs start with vault/, and a certificate file is required.
Both: secrets synced from your PAM solution (Privilege Cloud or PAM Self-Hosted).
limits: API key authentication only: the connector holds a secret zero. Protect it with secure properties and rotate it.
Read only: the connector cannot create, update or remove secrets.
Requires Java 8 or 11 and Mule SDK 4.4.0.
The secrets list is comma-separated and does not accept spaces.
At least one certificate file (.pem or .der) is required for Edge (SaaS) and for Self-Hosted.

flow.diagram_label: Animated diagram: a Mule flow authenticates with an API key, retrieves secrets and calls a backend
flow.s1_desc: The Mule application uses the Retrieve secret operation to get credentials from Secrets Manager when the flow runs.
flow.s2_desc: Account, URL, workload ID and API key come from conjur.properties through secure placeholders, not from values typed into the XML.
flow.s3_desc: Any REST client calls the deployed Mule application, and the flow reaches the Retrieve secret step.
flow.s4_desc: The connector sends the workload API key to Secrets Manager and receives an access token.
flow.s5_desc: With the token, the connector asks for the comma-separated list of secret IDs. Policy checks that the workload belongs to the Safe consumers group.
flow.s6_desc: The next step of the flow logs in to the backend with the values, and the Mule application answers the client.

sm_summon.title: Summon
sm_summon.subtitle: An open source CLI that fetches secrets from Secrets Manager and hands them to a process as environment variables, so they never live in source code, config files or shell history.
sm_summon.caps_lead: One small binary plus a provider. It works with any language, because the application only reads environment variables.

caps.title: Environment variables for a child process
caps.desc: Summon reads secrets.yml, fetches each !var and starts your command with the values injected. They exist only in that process and vanish when it exits.

caps.title: Files when an app needs them
caps.desc: Besides environment variables, Summon can write secrets to files in JSON, YAML or dotenv format, or render them through custom Go templates.

caps.title: Pluggable providers
caps.desc: The Secrets Manager provider is one of several: Summon also has providers for AWS S3 and AWS Secrets Manager, so the same secrets.yml pattern works across stores.

sm_summon.flow_title: How it works, step by step
sm_summon.flow_lead: Summon runs on the same machine as the command it wraps. The provider authenticates with the identity already configured there, fetches only what secrets.yml lists and starts the child process.

flow.diagram_label: Summon flow: secrets.yml, Summon and its provider, Secrets Manager, the child process and the target system
flow.s1_desc: secrets.yml maps environment variable names to Secrets Manager variable paths with the !var tag. It holds paths only, never values, so it can live in Git next to the code.
flow.s2_desc: Summon calls its Secrets Manager provider (summon-conjur), which authenticates with the identity already set up on the host, for example a CLI login or a host API key, and receives a short-lived access token.
flow.s3_desc: For each !var the provider requests the value. Policy must grant the identity execute (or update) on the variable, and every fetch is written to the audit trail.
flow.s4_title: Start the child with the values
flow.s4_desc: Summon starts the wrapped command, for example terraform apply, with the values as environment variables. With Terraform, names use the TF_VAR_ prefix so they become Terraform variables.
flow.s5_desc: The application reads DB_PASSWORD like any environment variable and connects. No SDK and no code change are needed.
flow.s6_title: Process ends, secrets go with it
flow.s6_desc: When the child exits, its environment is gone. Nothing was written to disk, and on the next run Summon fetches the current value again, so rotations are picked up at restart.

sm_summon.roles_lead: Every piece lives outside your application code.
roles: secrets.yml
Declares environment variable names and the Secrets Manager paths behind them (!var). Safe to commit: it carries no values.
Summon
Open source CLI from Palo Alto Networks. Parses secrets.yml, calls the provider, then starts the child process with the values.
Provider (summon-conjur)
Small executable that talks to Secrets Manager: authenticates with the host identity and fetches each variable.
IDIRA Secrets Manager
Checks the identity and the policy (execute or update on each variable), returns the values and records every fetch in the audit trail.
Child process
Any command: terraform, a script, a systemd service. Reads secrets as plain environment variables.
sm_summon.example_lead: From the docs: map the TF_VAR_ names in secrets.yml, declare the variables in the manifest (variable "access_key" {}) and wrap the command. The second line shows the inline form used in a systemd ExecStart.
when: You already use Summon in the organization and want the same pattern for Terraform, scripts or services.
Legacy apps or scripts that read environment variables and cannot take an SDK.
systemd services: wrap ExecStart so the password is fetched at every start and never stored on disk.
Ansible managed nodes: the Secrets Manager Ansible role installs Summon on each node for local retrieval.
CI steps and local development, where a one line wrapper beats changing code.
sm_summon.diff_lead: Summon is the lightest path. When a native integration exists, the docs usually point to it first.
diff: Terraform
The docs recommend the Secrets Manager Terraform provider if you are not already familiar with Summon. The Summon route needs no installation besides Summon itself.
Kubernetes
Prefer Secrets Provider, the CSI driver or ESO. Summon can run inside a pod next to the Kubernetes Authenticator Client, which supplies the identity.
SDK or REST API
SDKs give per call control (refresh, error handling). Summon fetches once at start: a rotated value is only seen on the next run.
Edition
Works with Self-Hosted and SaaS: Summon is a client tool and only needs a reachable Secrets Manager plus an identity with access.
limits: Values are read once, when Summon starts the child. A long running process keeps the old value after a rotation until it restarts.
Environment variables are visible to the process, its children and anyone who can inspect that process on the host. Restrict host access accordingly.
Summon does not authenticate by itself: the provider relies on an identity already configured on the machine (CLI login, host API key or another supported method).
The identity needs execute or update privilege on every variable listed in secrets.yml, granted with permit statements in policy.
Summon is open source and versioned on its own (0.13.0 is listed with Self-Hosted 13.10). Install it from the GitHub repository; it is not part of the server.

sm_audit.title: Audit and SIEM
sm_audit.subtitle: Every authentication, secret fetch and policy change leaves an event. See where those events land in Self-Hosted and in SaaS, and how they reach your SIEM.
sm_audit.caps_title: What the audit trail gives you
sm_audit.caps_lead: Accountability for machine identities: who (user or host) did what, on which resource, from where, and whether it worked.

caps.title: Who, what, which resource
caps.desc: Events tell whether the requester is a host or a user and carry the full ID of the resource involved, for example the variable that was fetched.

caps.title: Standard formats
caps.desc: Self-Hosted follows Syslog RFC 5424 and also writes one JSON event per line. SaaS events live in the Audit service and export as CSV or through the SIEM API.

caps.title: Built for detection
caps.desc: Send events to Splunk or another SIEM and alert, for example, when a host keeps trying to fetch a secret it is not allowed to read.

sm_audit.flow_lead_sh: Self-Hosted: the Leader and every Follower produce events; the Leader aggregates them and exposes files for your SIEM.
sm_audit.flow_lead_saas: SaaS: events go to the platform Audit service; your SIEM pulls them through an API or the Splunk add-on.

flow.diagram_label_sh: Self-Hosted audit flow: workload, Follower, Leader, audit files and SIEM
flow.diagram_label_saas: SaaS audit flow: workload, Edge, Secrets Manager SaaS, Audit service and SIEM
flow.sh_s1_desc: The request hits a Follower, which serves reads. It generates a Fetch Secret Value event. Followers only produce events for read operations such as Login, Authenticate, Check Permission and Fetch.
flow.sh_s2_title: The Follower keeps a local copy
flow.sh_s2_desc: Secrets Manager writes the event to syslog-ng over a UNIX socket, which writes audit.log and audit.json locally. Nothing is lost if the Follower loses contact with the Leader.
flow.sh_s3_title: Forwarded to the Leader over mTLS
flow.sh_s3_desc: syslog-ng forwards the event to the Leader on port 1999 with mutual TLS, and sends an empty MARK message every 30 seconds to keep the connection alive through proxies and load balancers.
flow.sh_s4_desc: On the Leader, events from the whole cluster land in a dedicated internal Postgres audit database on port 5433. That is what the Secrets Manager UI searches.
flow.sh_s5_desc: The Leader also writes every event to /var/log/conjur: audit.log in Syslog format and audit.json with one JSON event per line. logrotate rotates both daily and deletes compressed files after 30 days by default.
flow.sh_s6_desc: Mount /var/log/conjur on the host and point a forwarder at audit.json. In Splunk, choose _json as the source type and every field is parsed.
flow.sh_s7_desc: When a host keeps trying to fetch a secret it has no access to, the failure events reach the SIEM and an alert can go straight to the security team.
flow.saas_s1_desc: Secrets Manager SaaS records the request as an audit event, here fetch-fetch. Other examples: authn-authenticate, update-update, policy-add, policy-change and policy-remove.
flow.saas_s2_title: The event reaches the Audit service
flow.saas_s2_desc: Events go to the platform Audit service, where the Activities page lists them with timestamp, event, username, action and service.
flow.saas_s3_desc: Only users with the Global auditor role see the Audit service. They filter by day, week, month or a custom range and create CSV reports of up to 10,000 rows each.
flow.saas_s4_desc: A service user tied to an OAuth2 client credentials app gets a token and calls the SIEM integration API, which returns events from the previous 7 days. Splunk can use the Audit add-on instead, and plugins exist for QRadar and Sentinel.
flow.saas_s5_title: Edge: forwarded calls are audited, Edge logs stay local
flow.saas_s5_desc: Requests that an Edge forwards to SaaS produce events in the Audit service. The Edge machine's own audits and logs are not there: collect them on the Edge itself.

sm_audit.roles_lead_sh: Self-Hosted: syslog-ng on every node, aggregation on the Leader.
sm_audit.roles_lead_saas: SaaS: the platform keeps the trail; you consume it.
roles_sh: Generate events for API requests. Followers have a read-only database, so they only produce read events (login, authenticate, check permission, fetch).
Receives events over a UNIX socket, writes audit.log and audit.json and forwards Follower events to the Leader over mTLS on port 1999.
Internal Postgres on port 5433 with the events of the whole cluster. The UI uses it to search audit events.
Rotates audit files daily (or above 40 MB), compresses the previous day and deletes files after 30 days. Configured in /etc/logrotate.d/conjur-audit.
Reads audit.json (or audit.log) from the host mount, for example with a Splunk universal forwarder.
Do not serve traffic, so they produce no events unless promoted to Leader.
roles_saas: Creates an event for every request, including requests forwarded by an Edge.
Platform service with the Activities page and Activities reports (CSV).
Identity Administration role required to see the Audit service tile.
OAuth2 Server web app (jwtRS256 tokens, scope isp.audit.events:read) plus a confidential client user that your SIEM uses to call the API.
Pulls events through the SIEM integration API, the Splunk add-on (Splunkbase) or the QRadar and Sentinel plugins.
Keeps its own audits and logs on the Edge machine.
sm_audit.events_lead_sh: Self-Hosted event messages and what triggers them. Read-only events are the only ones a Follower can emit.
sm_audit.events_lead_saas: Examples of SaaS audit event names, from the Audit documentation.
events_sh: Log in with username and password (read-only)
Check that an authenticator is configured (read-only)
Check whether a role can perform an action on a resource (read-only)
Retrieve the value of a secret (read-only)
Add a new value to a secret
Load a policy that creates, updates or deletes a policy object
when: Compliance evidence: prove which workload read which secret, and when.
Forensics after an incident: trace a leaked credential back to the hosts that fetched it.
Detection: alert on repeated denied fetches or unexpected policy changes.
Troubleshooting: see failed authentications and why a workload cannot read a variable.
diff: Where events live
Self-Hosted: audit database plus audit.log and audit.json on the Leader (Followers keep local copies). SaaS: the platform Audit service.
Format
Self-Hosted: Syslog RFC 5424 plus JSON lines. SaaS: Activities view, CSV reports and the SIEM API.
Getting events to a SIEM
Self-Hosted: forward the files from the host mount. SaaS: OAuth2 service user and SIEM API, Splunk add-on, or QRadar and Sentinel plugins.
Retention
Self-Hosted: logrotate settings (30 days by default) plus whatever your SIEM keeps. SaaS: the SIEM API looks back 7 days and generated reports stay listed for 30 days, so pull events continuously.
Who can see them
Self-Hosted: the Secrets Manager UI audit search and whoever can read the files on the host. SaaS: users with the Global auditor role.
limits_sh: Audits collected on the Leader are local and not replicated to other nodes: export them to a central system.
Default retention on disk is 30 days (daily rotation, or earlier when a file exceeds 40 MB). Customize /etc/logrotate.d/conjur-audit on the Leader and copy it to every Standby and Follower.
Standbys produce no events unless promoted to Leader.
Since version 13.10 the free text body of membership, members and resources events uses JSON for query parameters: update parsers, or read the structured_data fields.
Docker deployments must mount /var/log/conjur on the host so a forwarder can read the files (the AMI already does).
limits_saas: Only users with the Global auditor role see the Audit service.
Edge audits and logs are not in the Audit service; they stay on the Edge machine.
Activities reports are capped at 10,000 rows, exclude the last 24 hours, and at most ten reports run at once per region.
The SIEM integration API returns events from the previous 7 days only.
The Splunk add-on uses AWS IoT authentication and is not available in eu-south-1 (Milan), ap-southeast-3 (Jakarta) and il-central-1 (Tel Aviv).

cp_zos.title: Credential Provider for z/OS
cp_zos.subtitle: Mainframe jobs and programs get passwords from the Vault at run time instead of keeping them in JCL, datasets or code. A local provider on each LPAR caches them and reaches the Vault through the Central Credential Provider.
cp_zos.caps_lead: The same model as the other Credential Providers, adapted to z/OS: a started task, JCL friendly SDKs and a Windows Central CP as the bridge.

caps.title: Java and C/C++ SDKs
caps.desc: Jobs call clipasswordsdk.jar from JCL (request in SYSIN, password in CREDOUT) or link the C/C++ SDK natively or under USS.

caps.title: Persistent secure cache
caps.desc: Passwords, application details and access rules are cached encrypted on the LPAR and refreshed every 180 seconds by default, so jobs keep running if the Vault or the network is down.

caps.title: Rotation in sync
caps.desc: The CPM marks passwords before a scheduled change; the provider then reads them from the Vault instead of the cache, so it never hands out a stale password.

cp_zos.flow_title: How it works, step by step
cp_zos.flow_lead: Pick the PAM back end. On z/OS every Vault operation goes through the Central Credential Provider on Windows IIS.

flow.diagram_label_sh: z/OS Credential Provider flow with PAM Self-Hosted: job, z/OS provider, Central Credential Provider, Digital Vault, CPM and target system
flow.diagram_label_saas: z/OS Credential Provider flow with Privilege Cloud: job, z/OS provider, Central Credential Provider, Privilege Cloud, CPM and target system
flow.s1_desc: A batch job needs a database or FTP password. Instead of a dataset or a hardcoded value, it asks the z/OS Credential Provider, a started task on the same LPAR.
flow.s2_title: The job asks through the SDK
flow.s2_desc: A job step runs clipasswordsdk.jar through the JZOS launcher. SYSIN carries the AppID and a query (Safe, PolicyID, Username, Address), sent to the provider on port 18923.
flow.s3_desc: The application must be defined in the Vault with access to the Safe. On z/OS the provider checks allowed machines and the OS user; path, hash and certificate methods are not available.
flow.s4_title: Secure channel to the Central CP
flow.s4_desc: The provider reaches the Central Credential Provider web service over HTTPS, and a client certificate (mTLS) can be added. Plain HTTP works but is not recommended.
flow.s5_title: The Central CP fetches from the Vault
flow.s5_desc: The Central Credential Provider retrieves the password from the Vault or Privilege Cloud, which logs the access. The z/OS provider keeps it in its encrypted persistent cache.
flow.s6_desc: The provider returns the password and the SDK writes it to the CREDOUT dataset. The docs advise restricting that dataset and keeping it only as long as needed. The provider logs the request.
flow.s7_desc: The next job step uses the password on the target, for example an FTP transfer or a database login.
flow.s8_desc: Before a scheduled change the CPM marks the password (ChangeNotificationPeriod), changes it on the target and stores it. On its next refresh the provider sees the mark and reads the password from the Vault instead of the cache.

cp_zos.roles_lead: Every z/OS LPAR runs its own provider; the Central CP serves all of them.
roles: Batch job or program
Calls the Java SDK (clipasswordsdk.jar, IBM JVM 1.8) or the C/C++ SDK against the provider on the same LPAR.
z/OS Credential Provider
Started task (STC) in the system PROCLIB, running under a UID 0 user. Authenticates applications, keeps the encrypted cache and writes audit, console and trace logs.
Central Credential Provider
Windows Credential Provider plus web service on IIS, which can be load balanced. Performs every Vault operation for the z/OS providers.
Digital Vault or Privilege Cloud
Stores the accounts in Safes, holds the application definitions and logs every access.
CPM
Changes and verifies passwords on the targets and marks them before a change so caches stay in sync.
PVWA
Web interface where you define applications, accounts and their dependencies.
cp_zos.jcl_title: Example: request a password from JCL
cp_zos.jcl_lead: From the docs. SYSIN holds the request; CREDOUT receives the password and should be a fixed blocked sequential dataset.
when: Mainframe batch jobs (FTP, database, file transfer) that today read passwords from datasets or JCL.
Compliance programs that require regular password changes on z/OS without editing jobs.
Sites that already run a Central Credential Provider and want to extend it to the mainframe.
Business critical jobs that must keep running during a Vault or network outage (persistent cache).
cp_zos.diff_lead: The mainframe side is identical; what changes is where the Vault lives.
diff: Vault
Self-Hosted: Digital Vault v12.2 or later in your data center. Privilege Cloud: the SaaS Vault.
Minimum versions
z/OS Credential Provider 14.2 needs Central Credential Provider 14.2 or later. With Privilege Cloud, z/OS based providers are supported only from version 14.2.
Central CP
Always yours: installed on Windows IIS in your network, in both models.
CPM
Self-Hosted: your CPM server. Privilege Cloud: the CPM on the Privilege Cloud Connector.
Connectivity
z/OS providers only talk to the Central CP; the Central CP talks to the Vault.
limits: Supported z/OS versions: 2.5, 3.1 and 3.2, with IBM Java 8, SMP/E V3R6 or later, IBM XML Toolkit V1.11 and JZOS.
IPv4 only.
One provider per LPAR, and the SDKs only talk to a provider on the same LPAR.
Application authentication is limited to allowed machines and OS user: no path, hash or certificate methods.
The STC must run under a UID 0 user, and changes to local_appprovider.conf need a provider restart.
Rotation sync does not cover one-time password policies (MinValidityPeriod) or Exclusive Safes. ChangeNotificationPeriod must be at least three times the combined refresh intervals.
Clocks on the z/OS server and the Vault must be synchronized to UTC (for example with NTP).
External processes using the SDKs (CICS, IMS, WAS) can affect provider performance.
cp_zos.limits_source: Source: z/OS Credential Provider system requirements (docs)
cp_zos.config_lead: Validated at startup: an invalid value stops the provider and the error shows in the console log.
config: 18923. Where the provider listens for SDK requests.
URL of the Central Credential Provider web service. Replace the default before the first start.
None (Vault on every request) or Persistent (encrypted file plus memory, survives restarts).
appprovider_cache.db, used with the Persistent level.
Set in the CPM password policy: at least 3 times the provider plus Central CP refresh intervals (600 s and 400 s give 3000).

cmp.title: Compare products, use cases and technologies
cmp.subtitle: Start with the four products side by side, then pick one product to compare its use cases and technologies on the same dimensions: identity, delivery, code changes, rotation, availability and limits.
cmp.glance_lead: What each product solves, who consumes it and where the credential lives. Select a product name to open its overview.

sm.problem: Secrets hardcoded in code, images, config files and pipelines.
sm.consumer: Workloads: applications, pods, pipelines, scripts and AI coding tools.
sm.identity: The workload proves who it is with a native identity (Kubernetes JWT, cloud IAM, CI OIDC token, certificate) or an API key; policy decides what it can read.
sm.where: In Secrets Manager, either stored there or synced from PAM Safes (data/vault).
sm.usecases: Kubernetes, CI/CD, platforms, Summon, dynamic secrets, certificates (SaaS).
sm.choose: Applications and pipelines need secrets at run time without storing them.

swa.problem: Workloads that share static secrets to prove who they are.
swa.consumer: Workloads on Kubernetes, VMs and cloud, and AI agents.
swa.identity: SPIFFE IDs: X.509-SVID and JWT-SVID issued after attestation by the SWA Agent and renewed before they expire.
swa.where: No stored credential: short-lived SVIDs. A JWT-SVID can be exchanged for secrets in Secrets Manager or for cloud credentials.
swa.editions: A feature of Secrets Manager SaaS, US-EAST-1 region only.
swa.usecases: Service-to-service mTLS, cloud federation (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud), secret exchange, AI agents.
swa.choose: The target can verify SPIFFE or OIDC tokens and you want to remove the secret zero.

cp.problem: Privileged account passwords hardcoded in applications, application servers, scripts and mainframe jobs.
cp.consumer: Applications on their servers, application servers (JDBC), remote scripts and z/OS jobs.
cp.identity: An application ID (AppID) plus registered characteristics: allowed machines, OS user, path, hash or client certificate.
cp.where: In Vault Safes, rotated by the CPM and kept in an encrypted local cache.
cp.usecases: Credential Provider, ASCP, Central Credential Provider, z/OS, Dual Accounts.
cp.choose: Traditional applications that use privileged accounts managed in PAM.

shub.problem: Secrets spread across cloud stores with no central rotation policy or audit.
shub.consumer: Applications that read AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault natively.
shub.identity: Applications keep their cloud identity. Secrets Hub writes to each store with an IAM role, federated identity, Workload Identity Federation or a JWT/OIDC role.
shub.where: The source of truth is a PAM Safe; the target stores hold synced copies (one-way sync).
shub.editions: SaaS service. Source: Privilege Cloud or PAM Self-Hosted 11.5 or later (through a connector).
shub.usecases: Sync PAM secrets to cloud stores; discover and review the secrets already in those stores.
shub.choose: Developers must keep native cloud SDK calls while security keeps rotation and audit in PAM.

cmp.shub_limits_title: Integration limitations that apply to every target
shub_limits: Keys and certificates are not supported, only secrets. Dual accounts are not supported.
One-way sync: manual changes in a target are not detected and can be overwritten.

cmp.source_note: Values summarize each linked page, which cites the official documentation. Not documented means the documentation does not state it.

sdk.name: SDK (Spring Boot)
sdk.identity: Pod ServiceAccount JWT sent to authn-jwt.
sdk.delivery: The app calls the REST API and keeps values in memory (5 minute cache in the demo).
sdk.code: Yes: SDK or REST calls in the application.
sdk.rotation: Next fetch after the cache expires; no restart.
sdk.best: Java services that want control and per-secret audit.

sidecar.name: Sidecar (.NET)
sidecar.identity: Pod ServiceAccount JWT, presented by the Secrets Provider sidecar.
sidecar.delivery: The sidecar writes a Kubernetes Secret; the app reads environment variables (secretKeyRef).
sidecar.rotation: The sidecar keeps the Secret updated; environment variables need a restart (Reloader).
sidecar.limit: Values also exist as a Kubernetes Secret object.
sidecar.best: Polyglot apps that must not change code.

eso.name: External Secrets Operator
eso.identity: ServiceAccount JWT (audience conjur) used by the SecretStore.
eso.delivery: ExternalSecret syncs into a Kubernetes Secret; pods load it with envFrom.
eso.rotation: Refresh every minute in the demo; environment variables need a rolling restart.
eso.limit: The value is stored as a Kubernetes Secret.

csi.name: CSI Driver
csi.identity: Projected ServiceAccount token (audience conjur) used by the provider.
csi.delivery: Files on a read-only tmpfs volume; no Kubernetes Secret.
csi.code: Read files from the mount path.
csi.rotation: The rotation reconciler rewrites the volume (every 2 minutes in the demo); no restart.
csi.limit: The app must read files, not environment variables.

spmodes.name: Secrets Provider modes
spmodes.identity: authn-jwt, authn-iam, authn-azure, authn-gcp; Self-Hosted adds authn-k8s.
spmodes.delivery: Kubernetes Secrets or Push-to-File; init container, sidecar, Job or standalone.
spmodes.rotation: Only the sidecar and standalone update after start.
spmodes.limit: Push-to-File only with init container and sidecar; fetch all is capped at 500 secrets.
spmodes.best: Choosing the right deployment for each app.

reloader.name: Reloader
reloader.identity: Does not talk to Secrets Manager; watches Kubernetes Secrets.
reloader.delivery: Rolls the Deployments and StatefulSets that reference a changed Secret.
reloader.rotation: Automatic rollout when the Secret changes.
reloader.limit: Needs the Secrets Provider Helm chart in application or standalone mode.
reloader.best: Apps reading environment variables that must pick up rotated values.

secretless.name: Secretless Broker
secretless.identity: authn-k8s with a Follower in the cluster.
secretless.delivery: The app connects to a local broker, which adds the credential to the connection.
secretless.code: Point the connection at localhost, with no credentials.
secretless.rotation: The broker uses current values; no restart.
secretless.limit: Self-Hosted only; supported protocols only (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MSSQL, SSH, HTTP).
secretless.best: Apps that must never see the password.

gha.name: GitHub Actions
gha.identity: GitHub OIDC JWT bound to repository and workflow.
gha.delivery: The action fetches values as environment variables masked in logs.
gha.code: One workflow step plus permissions id-token: write.
gha.rotation: Each run fetches the current value.
gha.limit: Any repository or workflow that does not match the host annotations is denied.
gha.best: GitHub pipelines with no stored credential.

jenkins.name: Jenkins
jenkins.identity: A 2 minute JWT signed by Jenkins, verified through its JWKS endpoint.
jenkins.delivery: The plugin injects environment variables inside withCredentials, masked in logs.
jenkins.code: withCredentials with credential IDs in the Jenkinsfile.
jenkins.rotation: Each build fetches the current value.
jenkins.limit: Plugin v3.x requires Jenkins 2.455 or later.
jenkins.best: Jenkins pipelines with Global, Folder or Job credentials.

ansible.name: Ansible
ansible.identity: JWT from your IdP; API key, AWS IAM, Azure and GCP are also supported.
ansible.delivery: The lookup plugin resolves the value at play time on the control node.
ansible.rotation: Each run reads the current value.
ansible.limit: Tasks need no_log: true, or values can appear in output.

terraform.name: Terraform
terraform.identity: Provider authentication, for example JWT or API key (host_id when required).
terraform.delivery: Data sources or ephemeral resources read inside the manifest.
terraform.limit: Values are written to state unless ephemeral (1.10+) or write-only (1.11+).
terraform.best: Infrastructure pipelines, and managing Secrets Manager as code.

gitlab.name: GitLab CI/CD
gitlab.identity: GitLab ID token (JWT) whose aud matches the authenticator.
gitlab.delivery: A binary prints each secret to STDOUT and the script captures it.
gitlab.code: One call per CONJUR_SECRET_ID in the job script.
gitlab.rotation: Each job fetches the current value.
gitlab.limit: Images only for Alpine, Ubuntu and UBI-FIPS; one call per secret.
gitlab.best: GitLab pipelines tied to project and branch.

azdo.name: Azure DevOps
azdo.identity: Entra ID token through an Azure Resource Manager service connection (JWT); API key also supported.
azdo.delivery: A batch of secrets from secrets.yml becomes environment variables.
azdo.rotation: Each run fetches the current value.
azdo.limit: Read only: it cannot create, update or remove secrets.
azdo.best: Azure Pipelines that already have an Azure identity.

bitbucket.name: Bitbucket Pipelines
bitbucket.identity: Bitbucket OIDC JWT per step; the workload is the repository UUID.
bitbucket.delivery: Written to secrets.env and exported by load_secrets.sh.
bitbucket.code: Add the pipe to the step.
bitbucket.rotation: Each run fetches the current value.
bitbucket.limit: The file is readable by every process in the step; only _ is allowed as a special character.

circleci.name: CircleCI
circleci.identity: CircleCI OIDC token signed for your organization.
circleci.delivery: The orb exports the listed secrets as environment variables.
circleci.rotation: Each job fetches the current value.
circleci.limit: The audience must be your CircleCI organization ID.
circleci.best: CircleCI projects that should stop storing secrets in contexts.

octopus.name: Octopus Deploy
octopus.identity: JWT from a Generic OIDC account (audience conjur).
octopus.delivery: Each secret becomes an output variable for the next steps.
octopus.rotation: Each deployment fetches the current value.
octopus.limit: One missing or inaccessible secret fails the whole step (SaaS guide).

python.name: Python and AWS Lambda
python.identity: SDK: API key on SaaS; Self-Hosted also LDAP and JWT. AWS IAM client: the instance IAM role.
python.delivery: The SDK returns values to the code (get, get_many).
python.limit: The IAM client token is not refreshed (5 to 8 minutes) and is read only.
python.best: Python on EC2 with no secret zero, and automation.

cf.name: Cloud Foundry / Tanzu
cf.identity: The Service Broker creates one host per app or per space.
cf.delivery: A buildpack (Summon) injects environment variables at start.
cf.rotation: Only after a restart or restage.
cf.limit: Self-Hosted only; one service instance per space.
cf.best: Tanzu Application Service and Cloud Foundry apps.

puppet.name: Puppet
puppet.identity: A host API key on each node.
puppet.delivery: The agent fetches at apply time with Deferred functions.
puppet.code: Use the module function in manifests.
puppet.rotation: Fetched again on each agent run (Deferred).
puppet.limit: Self-Hosted only; the node API key is a secret zero.

mulesoft.name: MuleSoft
mulesoft.delivery: The Retrieve secret operation inside a Mule flow.
mulesoft.code: Add the operation in Anypoint Studio.
mulesoft.limit: Read only, and the API key is a secret zero.
mulesoft.best: Mule integrations that keep credentials in properties files today.

summon.name: Summon
summon.identity: Uses an identity already configured on the machine.
summon.delivery: Environment variables or temporary files for a child process.
summon.rotation: Read once at start; a restart picks up the new value.
summon.limit: Environment variables are visible on the host.
summon.best: Legacy scripts, systemd services and Terraform via Summon.

mcp.name: MCP Server
mcp.identity: The developer signs in through Idira Identity OAuth2; the agent acts as that user.
mcp.delivery: The AI tool creates secrets and workloads and generates code that fetches them.
mcp.code: Generated SDK calls replace the literals.
mcp.rotation: Not applicable: the generated code fetches at run time.
mcp.limit: Beta, development only; no boundary between the agent and the user.
mcp.best: Moving hardcoded secrets out of code with an AI tool.

dynamic.name: Dynamic secrets
dynamic.identity: Any authenticator; the workload must be in the issuer consumers group.
dynamic.delivery: Each read creates a new AWS or GCP credential.
dynamic.rotation: Nothing to rotate: it expires after its TTL (15 minutes to 12 hours).
dynamic.limit: Cloud targets only: AWS on both editions, GCP on SaaS.
dynamic.best: Short-lived cloud access for jobs and workloads.

certs.name: Certificates
certs.identity: The workload must be in the issuer executors group.
certs.delivery: Issue (certificate and key) or sign (CSR only) through Certificate Manager.
certs.limit: SaaS only, with Certificate Manager as the back end.

mtls.name: X.509-SVID (mTLS)
mtls.identity: Attestation by the SWA Agent (k8s_psat, x509pop or AWS instance identity).
mtls.delivery: The Workload API on a local socket returns the X.509-SVID and the trust bundle.
mtls.rotation: The agent renews the SVID before it expires; no restart.
mtls.limit: TCP 8443 to the SWA Server must be reachable from every node.

jwtsm.name: JWT-SVID to Secrets Manager
jwtsm.identity: An RSA-signed JWT-SVID sent to the Secrets Manager JWT authenticator.
jwtsm.delivery: Exchanged for an access token; the workload reads only the secrets policy grants.
jwtsm.code: Fetch the SVID, then call the REST API.
jwtsm.rotation: SVIDs renew automatically; secrets are read at request time.
jwtsm.limit: RSA signatures only; new identities have no secret access until granted.
jwtsm.best: Targets that are not SPIFFE-aware and still need a password.

aws.name: SVID to AWS (S3 demo)
aws.delivery: The cloud returns temporary credentials (OIDC federation).
aws.rotation: Temporary credentials expire; a new SVID gets new ones.
aws.limit: The issuer URL must be public, unauthenticated HTTPS.

ai.name: AI agents
ai.identity: Attestation, then one JWT-SVID per audience.
ai.delivery: Secrets from Secrets Manager, a Claude API token, Gemini Enterprise (agentless flow).
ai.code: SDK federation settings; no API key in the code.
ai.rotation: Tokens are minted on demand and expire in minutes.
ai.limit: US-EAST-1 only; Claude API federation accepts JWT-SVIDs only.
ai.best: AI agents that should hold no API key.

cp.name: Credential Provider (CP)
cp.identity: AppID plus allowed machines, OS user, path and hash.
cp.delivery: A local SDK (Java, .NET, C/C++, CLI) answers from an encrypted cache.
cp.rotation: The background cache refresh picks up CPM changes.
cp.limit: An agent on every server; up to 10 applications per CP recommended.

ascp.name: Application Server CP (ASCP)
ascp.identity: Allowed machines, OS user, path and hash (no client certificate).
ascp.delivery: The JDBC driver proxy gets the credential for the data source.
ascp.code: None: a data source configuration change.
ascp.rotation: New connections use it after the next cache refresh.
ascp.limit: Supported application servers and databases only; JRE 1.8 or later.
ascp.best: WebSphere, WebLogic, JBoss and Tomcat data sources.

ccp.name: Central Credential Provider (CCP)
ccp.identity: AppID plus allowed machines, Windows OS user (IIS) or client certificate.
ccp.rotation: Background cache refresh (25 minutes by default) and CPM change notification.
ccp.limit: Windows IIS only; one password per call.
ccp.best: Applications where no agent can be installed.

zos.name: Credential Provider for z/OS
zos.identity: AppID plus allowed machines and OS user.
zos.delivery: The JCL SDK writes the password to CREDOUT, or the C/C++ SDK returns it.
zos.code: A JCL step or SDK call.
zos.rotation: The CPM marks the password and the provider reads it again; cache refresh every 180 seconds.
zos.limit: One provider per LPAR; z/OS 2.5, 3.1 or 3.2.

dual.name: Dual Accounts
dual.identity: Consumers query the VirtualUserName, not a specific account.
dual.delivery: Always returns the Active account, through a Credential Provider or Secrets Manager.
dual.rotation: The CPM changes only the inactive account, after the GracePeriod.
dual.limit: Rotation by the CPM only; GracePeriod must cover every consumer refresh.
dual.best: High load, critical apps that need rotation with no downtime.

src_pc.name: Privilege Cloud (SaaS)
src_pc.identity: The SecretsHub user is a member of each Safe to sync.
src_pc.delivery: Sync policies map Safes to target stores.
src_pc.rotation: Each CPM rotation is synced to every target.
src_pc.limit: SecretsHub user in up to 1,000 Safes; up to 1,000 accounts per Safe.
src_pc.best: Privilege Cloud Standalone and Shared Services customers.

src_pamsh.name: PAM Self-Hosted
src_pamsh.identity: The SecretsHub user (DAPService) in the Vault; a connector reaches PVWA.
src_pamsh.delivery: The connector reads accounts from PVWA over HTTPS; Secrets Hub writes them.
src_pamsh.rotation: Same path on each CPM rotation.
src_pamsh.limit: PAM 11.5 or later, a connector is always required, one load balancer in front of PVWA.

t_aws.name: AWS Secrets Manager
t_aws.identity: An IAM role that Secrets Hub assumes.
t_aws.limit: Names up to 512 characters; secrets managed by AWS cannot be changed.

t_azure.name: Azure Key Vault
t_azure.identity: An app registration with federated identity (no client secret).
t_azure.limit: Access policy model not supported (RBAC only); names up to 127 characters.

t_gcp.name: GCP Secret Manager
t_gcp.identity: Workload Identity Federation with a service account.
t_gcp.limit: Labels truncated to 63 characters; the replication policy cannot change later.

t_hcv.name: HashiCorp Vault
t_hcv.identity: A JWT/OIDC auth role; a connector is always required.
t_hcv.rotation: Synced after each CPM rotation, through the connector.
t_hcv.limit: KV version 2 only; the connector must sit in the Vault network.
